No. The `await fetch(...)` runs only inside the component script, and Astro's code fence guarantees that JavaScript is "fenced in": it executes on the server (at build time or on demand) and is stripped from the final page, so neither the URL nor the credentials reach the browser. The boundary is the `---` fence itself — everything above it is the component script (server-only), everything below is the component template that determines the HTML output. Only data you explicitly render from the script, such as `user.name`, appears in the HTML sent to visitors. Zero JavaScript is added by default since Astro components don't render on the client.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-components/

Reach for a server island (`server:defer`) when the section is personalized server-rendered content that needs no client-side interactivity; a `client:load` island is for components that must be interactive in the browser, and it ships and hydrates framework JavaScript.

The timing differs: with `client:load`, the component's HTML is generated as part of the normal page render, and its JS bundle loads and hydrates afterward in the browser. With `server:defer`, generating that component's HTML is deferred — you provide fallback content (e.g. a `slot="fallback"`), and the component renders later in its own isolated context outside the page request, streaming its HTML in when the slow authenticated request resolves, without delaying the rest of the page.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/server-islands/

Evaluate the `error` before rendering anything from it — the prop is typed `unknown`, so check `error instanceof Error` (or otherwise narrow it) first and return appropriate content based on the error thrown: ```astro --- interface Props { error: unknown; } const { error } = Astro.props; ---
{error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error"}
``` Order matters because evaluating first prevents both runtime errors from accessing properties on a non-`Error` value and the leaking of sensitive information — in particular, you should avoid displaying the error's stack, which reveals how your server code is structured. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-pages/

You're most likely rendering the error's `stack` (or the raw error object), which contains information about how your code is structured on the server — file paths, internal function names, and similar details. Evaluate the error first and render only an appropriate message instead, e.g. `error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error"` with a generic fallback, never the stack. Note this `error` prop only exists on `src/pages/500.astro` for on-demand rendered pages; prerendered pages don't have this custom error page.

```astro
<html>
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
  </head>
  <body>
    <slot />
  </body>
</html>
```

`rawContent()` is a synchronous function returning the raw Markdown source as a string; `compiledContent()` returns that same document compiled to an HTML string — and since Astro 5.0 it is an async function (top-level await was removed from Markdown modules), so it must be awaited. Interpolating `compiledContent()` without `await` yields a pending Promise, not HTML, so you'd render `[object Promise]` (or nothing useful) instead of your content. Await it first:

```astro
---
const content = await compiledContent();
---
<Fragment set:html={content} />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/upgrade-to/v5/

`getHeadings()` is a utility exported by an *imported* Markdown file (e.g. `import * as post from "../blog/post.md"`), not a prop Astro passes to layouts — layouts receive a plain `headings` array instead. Use `Astro.props.headings`, typed as `{ depth: number; slug: string; text: string }[]`: ```astro --- const { headings } = Astro.props; --- {headings.map(h => {h.text})} ``` You get the same data — depth, slug, text — without calling a function. The `config` object passed to a custom session driver’s implementation must be serializable because it is transmitted from the Astro configuration runtime (Node.js) to the session driver's runtime environment (e.g., Cloudflare Workers). If the config contains non-serializable values like functions or class instances, the driver will fail to initialize or behave unpredictably at runtime.

For example, passing a function in `config` would cause issues during serialization when the adapter tries to send it to the worker. The error message "The configuration of the logger is not serializable" applies here—non-serializable values in config lead to runtime failures because they cannot be passed across execution boundaries.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/session-driver-reference/

Delay the Avatar with the `server:defer` directive and provide a placeholder in the `fallback` slot; hydrate the React component only in view with `client:visible`:

```astro
<Avatar server:defer>
  <svg slot="fallback" class="generic-avatar" transition:name="avatar">...</svg>
</Avatar>

<ReactPokemonComponent client:visible />
```

`server:defer` makes the Avatar a server island: its server rendering is deferred so it streams in when ready without delaying the page, showing the fallback until then. `client:visible` is a `client:*` hydration directive: the React component first renders to static HTML on the server, and its JavaScript (plus React itself) is not sent to the browser until the user scrolls the component into view.

Yes, `.html` files are supported as Astro HTML components, but they must contain only valid HTML — so your template expression, import, and frontmatter are ignored (the expression renders as literal text). HTML components lack frontmatter, server-side imports, and dynamic expressions entirely. Your `<script>` tags are left unbundled, treated as if they had an `is:inline` directive, which is why they aren't processed by Vite and see only globals. They can only reference assets located in the `public/` folder. Rename the file to `.astro` if you need expressions, imports, or bundled scripts.

Astro treats the `<slot>` inside an HTML component as an Astro slot, exactly as it would in an Astro component, so it won't behave as a native custom-element slot. To get HTML Web Component slot semantics instead, add `is:inline` to that element:

```html
<slot is:inline></slot>
```

This makes Astro leave the slot alone so the browser's native custom-element slot assignment applies. Note the surrounding rules for HTML components: they must be valid HTML with no frontmatter, imports, or expressions, their `<script>` tags are unbundled (`is:inline` behavior), and assets must live in `public/`.

Use a server island (`server:defer`) for the dashboard panel and `client:load` for the React counter:

```astro
<DashboardPanel server:defer />
<Counter client:load />
```

The key difference at render time: a `server:defer` component defers its *server* rendering — it renders on the server when its data is available, streaming in without delaying the rest of the page (the panel hits your private database on the server). A framework component with `client:load` first renders on the server to static HTML, then its JavaScript is sent to the browser as the page loads, where it hydrates and becomes interactive. In short: `server:defer` delays server output; `client:load` delays nothing server-side but hydrates immediately on the client.

The frontmatter code fence is guaranteed to keep JavaScript "fenced in": Astro components don't render on the client, they render to HTML at build-time or on-demand, and all frontmatter code is stripped from the final page. The fetch to your private endpoint, the token, and the JSON import therefore run only on the server and never reach users' browsers — you can safely write sensitive or expensive code there.

The JSX component's client-side code reaches the browser only when you render it with a `client:*` directive (`client:load`, `client:idle`, `client:visible`, `client:media`, or `client:only`); the directive determines when that JavaScript is sent. Without one, the component contributes no client JavaScript.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-components/

Build your table of contents by mapping `headings` to links like `{h.text}`. The `compiledContent()` HTML will have matching `id` attributes on each heading because Astro injects IDs after plugins run, and the `slug` in `headings` reflects those final IDs. No additional coordination is needed.

`Astro.props` in a Markdown layout provides `headings` as an array of objects typed `{ depth: number; slug: string; text: string }[]`. You cannot call `getHeadings()`—the docs explicitly state heading information is available "via the `headings` array, rather than a `getHeadings()` function." Use `Astro.props.headings` directly to build your table of contents.

Use `rawContent()` for the original Markdown source (synchronous function returning a string) and `compiledContent()` for the rendered HTML string (async function returning a Promise<string>). `compiledContent()` is asynchronous; `rawContent()` is not.

`getHeadings()` is not available in Markdown layouts—it only exists on imported Markdown modules and content-collection `render()` results. In a layout, heading data is provided as the `headings` array on `Astro.props` (type `{ depth: number; slug: string; text: string }[]`). Access it via `Astro.props.headings` instead.

Astro treats `dependencies` and `devDependencies` the same at build time—both are installed and available. The docs recommend putting all dependencies in `dependencies` to start, only using `devDependencies` if you have a specific need. For `astro-icon` (imported in components during build), place it in `dependencies`.

The component script in the code fence runs only on the server (at build time or on demand), and all of it is stripped from the final page sent to the browser, so the `await fetch(...)` call and its token never reach the client. The imported React component's client-side code reaches the browser only when you render it with a `client:` directive (e.g. `<SomeReactComponent client:visible />`), which turns it into a hydrated "client island"; without a `client:` directive it renders only as static HTML with zero JavaScript.

Plain `.html` files must contain only valid HTML, so they lack key Astro features: no frontmatter, no server-side imports, and no dynamic expressions — meaning you cannot receive or use Astro props at all. Their `<script>` tags are also left unbundled (as if `is:inline`) and they can only reference assets in `public/`. Reach for an `.astro` component instead: Astro components support a frontmatter code fence where you access props via `Astro.props`, render them in the template, and still keep the rest of the page simple for non-framework editors.

Layout components conventionally live in a `src/layouts` directory, but this is not a requirement — you can place them anywhere in your project. They are ordinary Astro components with nothing special about them, and they can even be colocated alongside your pages in `src/pages` by prefixing the layout filename with `_` so it isn't treated as a route.
If a layout component contains a page shell, its `<html>` element must be the parent of all other elements in the component — every other element must be nested inside it.

Prefix the layout filename with an underscore (e.g. `src/pages/_Layout.astro`); the `_` prefix excludes that file from routing so it won't be generated as a page, letting you colocate the layout with your pages while still importing and using it like any other component.

Import the base layout in the blog post layout's frontmatter, wrap your post content and the `` inside it, and pass the needed props explicitly: ```astro --- import BaseLayout from './BaseLayout.astro'; const { frontmatter } = Astro.props; ---

Written by: {frontmatter.author}

 ``` Anything you pass as an attribute (e.g. `pageTitle`) is available in `BaseLayout` through `Astro.props`, and the original page's content flows into the blog layout's ``, which itself sits inside the base layout so it lands in the base layout's content area.

Because Astro components never render on the client: they render to HTML at build-time or on-demand, and the component script (the `---` frontmatter) is fenced so its JavaScript never escapes into the page sent to the browser. The result is a faster site with zero JavaScript footprint by default; interactivity is added only where needed via standard `<script>` tags or hydrated framework components as "client islands." This "fast by default" principle underlies Astro's server-first architecture.

Yes. Client islands run in isolation, but they can still share state and communicate across component contexts. Astro's recommended solution is Nano Stores: framework-agnostic stores under 1 KB with zero dependencies, so they work across React, Preact, Vue, Svelte, and Solid islands on the same page. Alternatives include Svelte built-in stores, Solid signals exported from a shared file, Vue's reactivity API, or custom browser events. Note that writing to a store from `.astro` frontmatter does not affect hydrated client components, and stores can't be passed as props to them.

An SPA is more appropriate when you need the simplicity and power of a full client-rendered application — for example, an app-like experience where the entire page is highly interactive, or an existing SPA embedded inside an Astro page (such as one migrated from Create React App). SPAs hydrate the whole site as one large JavaScript application, which causes page-load performance problems, and they lack the ability to selectively hydrate — making them a heavy-handed choice for most content-focused websites, where Astro's islands architecture wins.

Write `href="/authors/sonali/"` — a URL path relative to your root domain: ```astro Read more about Sonali. ``` Astro uses file-based routing: each file in `src/pages/` becomes a site endpoint based on its file path, so `src/pages/authors/sonali.astro` is served at `/authors/sonali/`. A relative file path like `../authors/sonali.astro` references the source-file system, not the deployed URL space — the browser has no knowledge of your `src/` directory, so the link would resolve to a nonexistent path.

Partials (added in `astro@3.4.0`) intentionally omit the `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration and all `<head>` content — including your component's scoped `<style>` and `<script>` tags — which is why they are stripped from the HTML output. Astro's guidance is to avoid partials when the component contains scoped styles or scripts; instead use a regular, non-partial page together with a frontend library (e.g. htmx) that knows how to merge the returned head contents into the document.

Pass your custom content to the named `"fallback"` slot on the `server:defer`-marked component:

```astro
---
import Avatar from '../components/Avatar.astro';
import GenericAvatar from '../components/GenericAvatar.astro';
---
<Avatar server:defer>
  <GenericAvatar slot="fallback" />
</Avatar>
```

The fallback content is rendered along with the rest of the page on initial load, then replaced with the island's real content once it arrives from its own route. Fallbacks can be generic avatars, custom messages, or loading indicators, and server islands require an installed adapter for the delayed rendering.

Astro’s semantic versioning contract does not protect against changes to experimental features because **experimental flags are explicitly exempt from stability guarantees**, even in patch releases.

When a feature is marked as experimental (like `incrementalBuild` or the Container API), it may change behavior, be removed, or have its API altered without notice — including in patch versions. This is by design, allowing Astro to iterate quickly on new functionality before stabilizing it.

You can safely assume that an experimental flag will not break your build only after it has been stabilized and moved out of the `experimental` config section. Until then, always check the [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/withastro/astro/blob/main/packages/astro/CHANGELOG.md) or release notes for breaking changes to experimental features.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/upgrade-astro/#semantic-versioning

`server:defer` keeps the rendering work on the server: the component's content is rendered on-demand on the server (deferred until its contents are available) and then fetched to the browser as HTML, without delaying the rest of the page. `client:load` moves the interactive rendering work to the browser: the component first renders to static HTML on the server, then its JavaScript (and the UI framework's JavaScript) is sent to the browser on page load, where it hydrates and becomes interactive. In short: server islands defer server-side rendering per component; `client:load` defers hydration to the client after load.

Mark the personalized elements (user avatar, special deals, reviews) with `server:defer`, so each renders independently and on-demand on the server, while the product description and images are rendered immediately as static HTML. Because the outer shell and main content do not depend on the dynamic parts, they can be cached far more aggressively—they change infrequently and do not vary per user. Each island is split into its own route and fetched in parallel at run time; generic fallbacks (generic avatar, announcements) display until personalized content arrives, so caching the static sections does not degrade the dynamic experience.

Only its server-rendered HTML (and any CSS) is sent—no component JavaScript and no React framework JavaScript. Without a `client:*` directive, Astro renders UI framework components to static HTML at build time or on-demand and strips the component's JavaScript from the final page; the browser receives plain HTML with no hydration. This is the default for all framework components: their HTML is rendered onto the page without JavaScript.

The mechanism is fallback content: children marked with `slot="fallback"` are rendered along with the rest of the page on initial load and are replaced by the island's real content when it arrives. Correctly sized fallback content is intended to prevent layout shift. It fails when the real content occupies a different amount of space than the fallback (for example, a longer name, a taller reviews list, or a different-sized image), or when no fallback is provided at all—so the reserved placeholder is the wrong size and the layout shifts once the island replaces it.

`client:idle` hydrates only after the page finishes its initial load and the `requestIdleCallback` event fires (falling back to the document `load` event in browsers that lack `requestIdleCallback`). Continuous scrolling keeps the browser busy, so the idle callback may never fire and the component stays unhydrated. Use `client:load` instead: it loads and hydrates the component JavaScript immediately on page load, with high priority, regardless of browser idle state.

Place it in the `public/` directory. Files in `public/` are not processed during Astro's build; they are copied into the build folder untouched, which makes that directory ideal for assets that must be served as-is, such as a downloadable PDF resume.

`src/components` holds reusable UI pieces (Astro, React, Vue, etc.) used across pages, while `src/layouts` holds page-template components that provide a shared shell (`<html>`, `<head>`, `<body>`) and a `<slot />` where page content is injected. Layouts are a specialized type of component used for whole-page structure; components are general-purpose reusable units.

Yes. The `src/styles` directory is only a convention — Astro processes and optimizes stylesheets from anywhere inside `src/` as long as they are imported correctly (e.g., `import '../styles/utils.css'`). Renaming it to `src/css` works without configuration changes.

`tsconfig.json` provides TypeScript configuration for the project. It is generated in every starter template and is required for full editor support — some features (like npm package imports) are not fully supported in the editor without it.

Add a `client:*` directive to the component usage in an Astro page. For example: `<MyReactComponent client:load />`. This tells Astro to hydrate that component as an interactive island while the rest of the page remains static HTML. Other directives like `client:idle` or `client:visible` control when the component loads.

"Independent" means each framework runs in its own isolated island context on the page. Multiple frameworks (React, Preact, Svelte, Vue, SolidJS) can coexist on the same page without interfering with each other; each island hydrates separately, and Astro handles the framework-specific transformations per component via file extension or explicit `include` configuration when JSX frameworks share extensions.

Astro supports running multiple frameworks simultaneously, so you can keep existing React components while adding new Svelte components on the same page. Import both frameworks' components into an `.astro` page and hydrate only the parts that need interactivity with `client:*` directives. This allows incremental replacement with no downtime — the rest of the page stays static HTML.

State does not transfer between them: each island runs in isolation in its own component context, so a framework-specific sharing mechanism (e.g. React context providers) cannot cross island boundaries and won't affect the other island. Sharing still works if you use a framework-agnostic client-side store such as Nano Stores, which both the React and Vue island import and subscribe to. Nano Stores are framework-agnostic, lightweight (<1 KB, zero dependencies), so sharing state between frameworks is seamless.

Astro compiles each framework component through its own integration—selected by file extension—and server-renders it to static HTML, so no framework runtime exists on the page until you opt in with a `client:*` directive. Because every island runs in isolation with no shared runtime, React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, etc. coexist without conflicts; when two hydrated components use the same framework, that framework's JS is sent only once. Only Astro components (`.astro`) may mix frameworks, and multiple JSX frameworks (React, Preact, Solid) are disambiguated with each integration's `include`/`exclude` options.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/preact/

MPA means Astro's server renders each page as its own HTML document (server-first, pre-rendered or on-demand), with client-side rendering added only where you opt in, whereas the SPA model builds the entire site in the browser using a client runtime, with SSR added mainly for performance. Astro says the SPA model's additional complexity and performance tradeoffs harm Time to Interactive (TTI), a metric that doesn't make much sense for content-focused websites where first-load performance is essential.

Because Astro components render only on the server (at build time or on-demand) to static HTML with no client-side runtime and no reactivity—Astro was designed to render on the server, not in the browser, so "there is no reactivity on the server" and hooks, stale closures, refs, observables, atoms and reactions have nothing to act on. That complexity only reappears if you explicitly opt into a hydrated UI-framework island or a client `<script>`.

"Opt in to complexity" means Astro removes required complexity by default: you can build a "Hello World" site with just HTML and CSS, then incrementally reach for new features and APIs as your needs grow. This directly serves the goal of being accessible to every web developer, since Astro was designed to feel familiar and approachable regardless of skill level—you don't need to be an expert to build something with Astro, and advanced capabilities are only adopted when you choose them.

Astro's content-driven, server-first design makes it a weaker fit: it prioritizes rendering HTML on the server with zero JavaScript by default and deliberately trades away the browser-centric model that heavy client state relies on. Complex, application-like experiences—logged-in admin dashboards, inboxes, social networks, todo lists—are what frameworks like Next.js and SvelteKit excel at. Astro is designed instead for content-rich websites: blogs, marketing sites, documentation, portfolios, landing pages, and e-commerce, where content must reach the reader quickly.

In Astro, features are marked as deprecated in minor releases (like v3.0) to warn users and provide time for migration. Removal occurs in major releases (like v4.0), where deprecated features are entirely eliminated from the codebase.

Deprecated features may still function temporarily but will eventually be removed. This process allows developers to update their projects gradually without sudden breaking changes.

Astro v3.0 removes APIs deprecated in earlier versions, while Astro v4.0 removes those deprecated in v3.x and earlier.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/upgrade-to/v3/

No, this is not a semver violation. According to Astro’s semantic versioning policy, patch releases can include bug fixes that may unintentionally break code relying on unintended or undesirable behavior, as long as those changes align with the documented functionality and expected behavior.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/upgrade-astro/#semantic-versioning

"Zero JavaScript by default" applies only to `.astro` components; hydrated UI framework components are the usual cause of a high Time to Interactive. Any framework component using a `client:*` directive ships that component's JavaScript plus its framework runtime (React, Svelte, etc.) to the browser, and with `client:load` the import begins as soon as the page loads, competing with interactivity for main-thread time. Choosing `client:visible`, `client:idle`, or `client:media` defers that cost, and skipping hydration entirely keeps it at zero. Note the framework bundle is shared: if multiple components use the same framework, it is sent only once.

The `create astro` wizard generates a project root containing `src/` (your pages, components, layouts, styles, images, and content), `public/` (unprocessed assets like `robots.txt` and `favicon.svg`), `package.json`, `astro.config.mjs`, and `tsconfig.json`. Only `src/pages/` is strictly reserved; the example tree also shows conventions like `src/components/`, `src/layouts/`, `src/styles/`, and `content.config.ts`, which you may rename or reorganize. The wizard additionally adds `dev`, `build`, and `preview` scripts to `package.json` (`astro dev`, `astro build`, `astro preview`) and can initialize a git repository and install dependencies when you accept those prompts.

`tsconfig.json` holds the TypeScript configuration options for your Astro project, and it is generated in every starter template. Without it, some features—specifically npm package imports—are not fully supported in the editor, so autocompletion and resolution for those imports degrade or fail. Create the file (or keep the one your starter provides) to restore full editor support; adjust compiler options via the TypeScript Guide.

No — pages must live in `src/pages/`; it is the only directory reserved (and required) by Astro, and without it your site has no routes. `app/routes/` cannot serve as the pages directory. Every other directory is merely convention: you are free to rename and reorganize `components`, `layouts`, `styles`, and similar folders however you like (though they typically live under `src/`, whose contents are processed and optimized by Astro).

No — a `<link>` to `public/styles/main.css` skips Astro's normal CSS processing, bundling, and optimizations. You get a consistent absolute URL and full manual control, but no minification, no per-page chunk splitting with shared-CSS reuse, and no automatic inlining of small stylesheets (production builds inline chunks under 4kB by default, controlled by `assetsInlineLimit` / `build.inlineStylesheets`). For bundling, import the stylesheet from `src/` in your component frontmatter: `import '../styles/utils.css';`. Also, relative `href` values are unsupported — the path must be absolute.

Astro uses a server-first Multi-Page App (MPA) approach, rendering HTML on the server by default, while Next.js uses a Single-Page App (SPA) model built for client-side rendering with SSR added for performance. You opt into client-side rendering for a component when it needs interactivity, using `client:*` directives (`client:load`, `client:visible`, `client:idle`, etc.) — this creates an interactive "island" while the rest of the page stays static HTML. `client:only` differs by skipping server rendering entirely for that component (requiring a framework hint), whereas regular `client:*` directives render on the server first, then hydrate on the client.

Return a generic fallback such as `"Unknown error"` instead of attempting to describe the unrecognized error. The `error` prop type is `unknown`; inspect it with `instanceof Error` first, and never expose `error.stack` to avoid leaking server internals.

Send the `Clear-Site-Data` response header on the response that confirms sign-out (e.g. your `/logout` redirect or its landing page), quoting each directive:

```http
Clear-Site-Data: "cache", "cookies", "storage", "executionContexts"
```

`"cookies"` clears cookies/auth for the registered domain, `"storage"` clears localStorage/sessionStorage/IndexedDB and unregisters service workers, `"cache"` clears the HTTP cache, and `"*"` clears everything. It requires HTTPS, must never be sent site-wide, and the values must be quoted.

Set the `HttpOnly` attribute on the cookie when you send it: `Set-Cookie: name=abc123; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax`. `HttpOnly` keeps the cookie out of `document.cookie`, so no client-side script in the page — including an XSS payload — can read it; the browser still sends it on requests. Also add `Secure` (HTTPS-only) and an explicit `SameSite` (usually `Lax`), and prefer the `__Host-` prefix for session cookies, which pins the name, `Secure`, `Path=/`, and no `Domain`. Only omit `HttpOnly` from cookies JavaScript genuinely needs to read, such as preferences or an A/B bucket.

`skewProtection` is a `boolean` option (Serverless only, added in `@astrojs/vercel@7.6.0`) that turns on Vercel Skew protection, keeping clients and server in sync during a deployment so users who load your site mid-deploy don't hit version mismatches. The header only affects the origin (and, for `"cookies"`, the registered domain including subdomains) that serves it, so correctness comes from scoping: send `Clear-Site-Data` only on the response that confirms sign-out — the `/logout` redirect or its landing page — never site-wide. A stray header on every response wipes the user's session on each request. Each directive must be a quoted token (e.g. `"cookies"`), and the header is ignored outside a secure context (HTTPS), so serve it over HTTPS only.

`"*"` clears everything — cookies, storage, caches, prefetch/prerender caches, and even data types added in future revisions of the spec — so on a logout response it can destroy state the user expects to keep (e.g. preferences in `localStorage`), and combined with site-wide sending it wipes the session on every request. Avoid it by enumerating only the directives you actually want gone, quoted, on the exact sign-out response:

```http
Clear-Site-Data: "cache", "cookies", "storage"
```

Also remember the header must be quoted and sent over HTTPS or it is ignored.

  domain: "example.com",
  maxAge: 60 * 60 * 24 * 30,
  secure: true,
  httpOnly: true,

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/api-reference/

The `__Host-` prefix is browser-enforced: the cookie name must start with `__Host-`, and the browser only accepts it if it is `Secure`, has `Path=/`, and has **no** `Domain` attribute — pinning the session cookie to the exact host and blocking a compromised subdomain from rewriting it (subdomain takeover defence). The implication is you cannot set a custom `domain` on such a cookie, so it won't be shared across subdomains; use it for session cookies whenever you can. In Astro, the session cookie options (`session.cookie`, added in `astro@5.7.0`) merge with defaults that already include `secure: true`, `httpOnly: true`, and `sameSite: "lax"`, so you can set `name: "__Host-astro-session"` and the attributes line up.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/security/cookie-attributes/

Send the `Referrer-Policy` header on every HTML response; the recommended baseline is `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`:

```http
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
```

This sends the full URL on same-origin requests, only the origin on cross-origin HTTPS requests, and nothing on HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrades. In on-demand rendering or server endpoints, include it in the headers of the `Response` you return, for example `new Response(html, { status: 200, headers: { "Referrer-Policy": "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" } })`, so every outgoing request is covered. Per-page or per-element overrides are possible with `<meta name="referrer" content="...">` or the `referrerpolicy` attribute.

Add the `referrerpolicy="no-referrer"` attribute directly to that link's `` element: ```html Partner ``` This per-element override makes the link send no referrer information at all, regardless of the site-wide policy. To suppress referrers for an entire page instead, use ``.

Common mistakes: using `unsafe-url` (always sends the full URL — avoid it); setting the header on only some responses instead of every HTML response, leaving other pages uncovered; and sending full URLs cross-site so paths and query parameters (e.g. `/account/reset?token=abc123`) leak to third parties. Prevent them by explicitly sending `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` — the recommended default — on every HTML response, tightening to `same-origin` or `no-referrer` on sensitive pages (password reset, account settings, internal tools), and using per-element `referrerpolicy` overrides for individual links that must send nothing.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/security/referrer-policy/

To restrict embedding to your own site, use `same-origin`. Available values are `same-origin`, `same-site`, and `cross-origin`, from most to least restrictive:

```http
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin
```

Because it is a response header, it applies to every resource response your site returns. `same-site` allows sibling pages on the same site; `cross-origin` permits any origin.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/security/cross-origin-isolation/

Send the `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` (COEP) response header on your documents with the value `require-corp` (or `credentialless`); `unsafe-none` is the default and provides no protection. COEP then requires every subresource your document loads to opt in via CORP or CORS, so your resources are never pulled into an attacker's process — the Spectre side-channel that would let a hostile page read other sites' data. Full cross-origin isolation also pairs COEP with `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and a suitable CORP value (`same-origin`, `same-site`, or `cross-origin`).

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/security/cross-origin-isolation/

Set the `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` (COOP) response header to `same-origin` on your pages. COOP places your document in its own browsing context group and severs the `window.opener` link, so a page on another origin can no longer reach back into your tab and silently replace it with a fake login screen (tabnabbing) or probe sites the user is signed in to. Use `same-origin-allow-popups` or the newer `noopener-allow-popups` if you must keep some opener relationships; `unsafe-none` is the default and blocks nothing.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/security/cross-origin-isolation/

- **Not supported in `dev` mode** (Vite dev server) — test with `astro build` and `astro preview`.
- **External scripts and external styles aren't supported out of the box** — provide your own hashes.
- **Astro's `<ClientRouter />` view transitions aren't supported** — migrate to the browser-native View Transition API if you aren't using Astro's enhancements to it.
- **Shiki isn't supported** — it emits inline styles that can't work with Astro's CSP; use `<Prism />` when you need both CSP and syntax highlighting.
- **`'unsafe-inline'` in a directive suppresses Astro's hashes** for that directive (browsers ignore hashes alongside it), reducing it to `'unsafe-inline'` strength — omit it to keep hash-based protection.

```js
security: { csp: { algorithm: 'SHA-512' } }
```

It affects security only in that your policy's script/style hashes are computed with the chosen function — it does not change which directives or sources your policy allows.

Reporting-Endpoints: default="https://example.com/reports", csp-endpoint="https://example.com/csp"
Content-Security-Policy: ...; report-to csp-endpoint
```

Each name maps to a URL that receives batched JSON violation reports; reports with no header of their own (deprecations, interventions, crashes) go to `default`. Because it must be a response header rather than a `<meta>` tag, it is sent by whatever serves your HTML (host/adapter), and the receiving collector can be an Astro endpoint in `src/pages` that returns a `Response`.

On the first page of a paginated route, `page.url.prev` is `undefined` because there is no previous page before the first one.

Similarly, `page.url.first` is also `undefined` on the first page since it's redundant to link to the first page when already on it.

The following `page.url` properties can be `undefined`:

- `page.url.prev`: When on the first page.
- `page.url.next`: When on the last page.
- `page.url.first`: When on the first page.
- `page.url.last`: When on the last page.

These values are only present when a corresponding adjacent page exists.

```

`Reporting-Endpoints` supersedes the never-standardised `Report-To` header and the CSP-only `report-uri` directive; it uses a simpler structured-header syntax and is the form to use today. Reports with no header of their own — deprecations, interventions, crashes — go to the endpoint named `default`. `max-age` is required — start with a short value to verify, then raise to two years (`63072000`). `includeSubDomains` extends the policy to every subdomain (audit them first). Do not include `preload`: the preload list's own operator now discourages it, and modern browsers auto-upgrade HTTP navigations to HTTPS anyway. - **`security.allowedDomains`** (array of `RemotePattern`, default `[]`, added `astro@5.14.2`): validates `X-Forwarded-Host` against patterns (supports `*.example.com` and `**.example.com`); when unset, the header is ignored.
- **`security.actionBodySizeLimit`** (number, default `1048576` / 1 MB, added `astro@5.18.0`): caps action request bodies.

CSP is configured under `security.csp` (added `astro@6.0.0`). The dev toolbar can be disabled with `devToolbar: { enabled: false }`.

{session.user?.name}

``` Hono middleware is the right tool for guarding whole route trees (e.g. everything under `/dashboard`) from a single place before Astro renders.

They are standard CSS units — use them directly in your `.astro` component `<style>` blocks or inline styles; no Astro configuration is required.

- `svh` (small viewport, toolbar shown) never overflows — use it for elements that must fit on first paint: heroes, login screens, modals.
- `dvh` (dynamic viewport) updates live as the mobile toolbar slides in and out — use it for elements that should track the visible area: bottom sheets, overlays' `max-height`.
- `lvh` (large viewport, toolbar retracted) equals the legacy `100vh`.

```css
.hero { min-height: 100svh; }
.sheet { max-height: 100dvh; }
```

Avoid `height: 100vh` on mobile — it resolves to the largest viewport, leaving content behind the URL bar. These units are Baseline-supported and replace the old JS `resize`-listener `--vh` workaround.

`svh` measures the small viewport (browser toolbar fully shown) and stays fixed; `dvh` measures whatever is visible right now and updates live as the mobile toolbar collapses and reappears while the user scrolls.

Use `svh` for elements that must always fit — landing heroes, login screens, modals — since `100svh` is the safe maximum that never overflows in any toolbar state. Use `dvh` for elements that should track the visible area as chrome moves, such as a bottom sheet or an overlay's `max-height`.

`100vh` resolves to the largest (retracted-toolbar) viewport, so it sits behind the URL bar and hides content. `lvh` behaves exactly like the old `vh`. All three are plain CSS, Baseline-supported, and need no JavaScript.

Filtering out unresolvable entries at the top of `getStaticPaths()` prevents broken pages from ever being generated.

If a resource is unavailable over HTTPS, the browser will fail to load it, even with this directive enabled.

Potential pitfalls include:

- **Broken functionality**: Resources like scripts or stylesheets may silently fail if their HTTP versions aren't available via HTTPS.
- **Mixed content blocking**: Active mixed content (e.g., scripts) is blocked outright by browsers regardless of `upgrade-insecure-requests`.
- **Legacy sites**: This directive helps legacy sites transition to HTTPS but cannot fix all insecure requests.

To avoid issues, ensure third-party resources are served over HTTPS or use a proxy that handles the upgrade. The best practice remains serving all subresources over HTTPS directly.

Native cross-document view transitions are declarative: each page opts in with `@view-transition { navigation: auto }`, no JavaScript — the browser captures page A, replaces it with B, and cross-fades, and you only shape it with `::view-transition-*` CSS. Use them sparingly — over-preloading makes resources compete for bandwidth and slows the LCP element. Complement them by streaming: move `await fetch()` calls into smaller components so data fetching doesn't block the rest of the HTML.

Use `preload` for any other late-discovered critical resource — an LCP image, a font referenced from CSS, styles — always with the correct `as=` (`image`, `font`, `style`, `script`, `fetch`). Both are plain `<link rel>` tags in your `<head>`; Astro adds no special handling. Don't preload too many resources: they fight for the same bandwidth and can delay the LCP element.

Use `view-timeline` (or the shorthand `animation-timeline: view()`) for per-element effects — reveal-as-you-scroll entrances, sticky-section pinning, per-element entrance animations — because progress tracks each element's own visibility instead of the container's scroll offset, which is what `scroll-timeline` suits (reading-progress bars, document-tied parallax. Pair it with `animation-range` to select the slice of the view timeline that drives the animation. Both run on the compositor.

`contain: strict` equals `size` plus `layout`, `paint`, and `style`, while `contain: size` alone only makes the element's own size computed without consulting its children. On its own, `size` provides no layout or paint isolation of descendants — it affects only intrinsic sizing, and without an explicit size or `contain-intrinsic-size` the box collapses to zero in the contained axis. `contain: strict` adds that sizing behavior on top of full rendering scoping, which is why `contain: content` (`layout paint style`, deliberately excluding `size`) is the recommended default for typical components. In an Astro component these properties behave exactly as in plain HTML.

No configuration is needed: the `<ClientRouter />` component includes a route announcer (added in `astro@3.2.0`) that automatically announces the new page title during client-side navigation. It adds an element to the new page with `aria-live` set to `assertive` so assistive technology announces immediately, and it determines the text in priority order: the `<title>` if present, otherwise the first `<h1>`, otherwise the page `pathname`. This mirrors what assistive technologies already do after a traditional full-page refresh, keeping client-side routing accessible — which is why each page should always include a `<title>`.

The `<ClientRouter />` includes a built-in CSS media query that disables *all* view transition animations — including the fallback animation — whenever the `prefers-reduced-motion` setting is detected; the browser then simply swaps the DOM elements with no animation. This requires no configuration and closes the accessibility gap that client-side routing creates: users susceptible to vestibular triggers never see transition motion, while others still get it. It applies automatically on top of the router's built-in route announcer, so opting into `<ClientRouter />` remains accessible-by-default — the same principle that requires authored motion (e.g. scroll-driven animations) to be gated on `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.

A bare `<script>` in `<head>` with no loading attribute halts HTML parsing while it downloads *and* executes, blocking first paint—on a slow network that can delay paint by seconds. With `defer`, the parser doesn't stop: the script downloads in parallel and runs in document order after parsing finishes, before `DOMContentLoaded`. With `async`, the parser doesn't stop either, but the script runs as soon as it arrives, in arrival order, possibly mid-parse. In an Astro project this matters because `<script>` tags are what ship JavaScript to the browser (frontmatter runs at build time and is discarded), and since Astro 5.0 scripts render exactly as declared—no longer hoisted to `<head>` or bundled together—so a blocking script stays wherever you author it. Use `defer` for your app code, `async` for independent third-party code.

Inline the above-the-fold CSS subset in a `<style>` tag in `<head>`, keeping it under ~14KB so it fits one TCP slow-start window, then load the rest asynchronously:

```html
<head>
  <style>/* ~14KB of styles for above-the-fold content */</style>
  <link rel="preload" href="/site.css" as="style" onload="this.rel='stylesheet'">
  <noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/site.css"></noscript>
</head>
```

Identify critical rules per page with tools such as `critical`, `penthouse`, or `critters` (build-time, per-page is better). Also move JavaScript off the critical path with `defer` or `type="module"`, use `async` only for independent third-party scripts, and don't put third-party stylesheets (webfonts, chat widgets) in `<head>`—self-host or load them asynchronously.

Both attributes keep the browser from stopping HTML parsing and download the script in parallel; they differ in execution timing. `defer` runs after the parser finishes, in document order, before `DOMContentLoaded`—right for your application code that depends on the DOM or on other scripts in order. `async` runs as soon as the file arrives, in arrival order, possibly mid-parse—only for self-contained third-party code like analytics or error reporters. In Astro, `is:inline` is implied whenever any attribute other than `src` is used, and an `is:inline` script is rendered as authored and not bundled into an external file, so attributes like `defer` that control loading of an external file have no effect. Also note that since Astro 5.0, scripts render as declared—no hoisting to `<head>`, no bundling of multiple scripts—so review your tags and their attributes accordingly.

Inspect the built output HTML: the `<head>` should contain no synchronous `<script>` lacking `async`, `defer`, or `type="module"`, and no plain `<link rel="stylesheet">`—critical CSS should be an inline `<style>` under ~14KB, with the full stylesheet loaded via the `preload` + `onload` swap plus a `<noscript>` fallback. Also confirm scripts aren't hoisted into `<head>`: since Astro 5.0, `<script>` tags render where declared (not hoisted, not bundled together, conditionally rendered scripts no longer implicitly inlined), so any blocking script you see is one you authored—review each tag and add `defer`/`type="module` (`async` only for independent third-party code) to keep JavaScript out of the critical path.

A `<script>` in `<head>` without `async`, `defer`, or `type="module"` halts HTML parsing while it downloads and executes, blocking both parsing and rendering—the single biggest cause of slow first paint. Prevent it by adding `defer` (parallel download, executes after parsing in document order, before `DOMContentLoaded`) or `type="module"` (deferred by default), using `async` only for truly independent third-party scripts. In Astro, JavaScript is sent to the browser only from `<script>` tags, and since Astro 5.0 tags render exactly as declared rather than being hoisted to `<head>`—and multiple scripts on a page are no longer bundled together—placing your script in the component body (e.g. just before `</body>`, as in the menu example) plus using `defer`/`type="module"` keeps it out of the render-critical path.

Domain sharding is net-negative under HTTP/2 and HTTP/3: it adds DNS lookups, TLS handshakes, and extra connections, and it defeats HTTP/2's single-connection coalescing — the very thing that makes multiplexed connections fast. QUIC's connection migration and 0-RTT only help when traffic stays on one origin, so sharding undermines those too. Sharding was invented to dodge HTTP/1.1's ~six-connections-per-origin limit, and HTTP/2/3 already multiplex unlimited concurrent requests over one connection, so the request-count problem it solved no longer exists. The fix is to consolidate assets onto a single origin and drop sharded hostnames like `cdn1.example.com`/`cdn2.example.com`.

`export const prerender = false` is required in any output mode other than `server` — i.e., in the default static mode where routes are prerendered — and is redundant in server mode, as the comment says. If you omit it there, the catch-all endpoint is built as a prerendered route instead of being rendered on demand, so `auth.handler(ctx.request)` never runs against live requests and your auth endpoints won't function at runtime. Keep the line unless the whole project uses `output: 'server'`.

Better Auth exposes its own HTTP surface: a catch-all API route (`src/pages/api/auth/[...all].ts`) forwards every request under `/api/auth/*` to `auth.handler(ctx.request)`, so the library owns routing and responses, and pages read session state server-side via `auth.api.getSession({ headers: Astro.request.headers })`. Clerk instead hooks the whole request pipeline: `clerkMiddleware()` set as `onRequest` in `src/middleware.ts` intercepts every page and endpoint before rendering and populates `locals`. Use API routes when you're serving a discrete endpoint that a library handles; use middleware when you need per-request auth state or route protection across the site. Clerk then exposes state through `const { isAuthenticated, userId } = locals.auth()` in pages/API routes (redirect or return 401), while its components (`<Show when="signed-in">`, `UserButton`, `SignInButton`) control visibility in the UI. Middleware can be combined with others via `sequence()`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/middleware/

Enable view transitions and apply the `transition:persist` directive to each input element. Inputs are cleared whenever a form is submitted, so preserving their values across a failing submission requires SPA-mode view transitions plus the directive on every `<input>`:

HTTP/3 is configured at your host or CDN, not by Astro. Check three things: your edge provider has HTTP/3 enabled (Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront, Bunny, and Akamai offer it as a toggle); you serve over HTTPS with a valid certificate, since browsers only use HTTP/3 over TLS; and your HTTP/2 responses advertise HTTP/3 via `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400`. Without that header, browsers never attempt an HTTP/3 connection.

Use the `defer` attribute or `type="module"` on the `<script>` tag — `defer` runs the script in document order after parsing finishes and before `DOMContentLoaded`, and `type="module"` is deferred by default. In Astro, note that any attribute other than `src` implies `is:inline`, and inline scripts are emitted as-is without bundling, so `defer`/`async` have no effect on them; an `is:inline` script must instead be placed appropriately in the document.

`is:inline` tells Astro to leave a `<script>` or `<style>` tag exactly as written in the final output HTML — the contents are not processed, optimized, or bundled. Use it when you need the tag emitted verbatim where authored, for example with conditionally rendered scripts, since Astro 5 no longer implicitly inlines them:

```astro
{showAlert && <script is:inline>alert("Some very important code!!")</script>}
```

The trade-offs: no npm imports, no compile-to-CSS languages, no relative `import`/`@import`/`url()` resolution, no deduplication, global unscoped styles, and loading attributes like `defer` have no effect. `is:inline` is also implied whenever any attribute other than `src` is used on a script or style tag.

Serve the site over HTTP/2 or later — some HTTP/1.1 intermediaries mishandle informational responses, and most clients act on Early Hints only on HTTP/2 or HTTP/3. In practice, set `Link` preload/preconnect headers on the final response for the few critical resources; many CDNs and edge platforms synthesize the `103` from those headers automatically (a configuration toggle rather than application code). Deploy on a platform that supports this — a static or adapter-enabled Astro site deploys to Vercel's edge network with zero configuration, and `vercel.json` can attach response headers. Repeat the same `Link` headers on the final response so clients that ignore `103` still get the hint, and hint sparingly.

Three common mistakes: (1) hinting resources the page doesn't actually use early, wasting bandwidth and warming the wrong connections — hint only the handful the page genuinely needs first (the LCP image, critical stylesheet, font origin); (2) sending `103` over HTTP/1.1, where some intermediaries mishandle informational responses — send it only over HTTP/2 or later; (3) over-hinting — twenty preloads just fight for bandwidth, so keep hints few. Also repeat the same `Link` headers on the final response, so clients that ignore `103` still receive the hints.

Brotli offers 15–25% better compression ratios than gzip for text resources like HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and JSON, resulting in smaller file sizes and faster load times. It is supported by all modern browsers.

To enable Brotli in Astro projects:

- Use a hosting provider or CDN that supports Brotli (e.g., Cloudflare, Fastly).
- Configure your server to prioritize brotli over gzip when serving static assets.
- Pre-compress static files at build time with brotli quality 11 and serve `.br` files directly.

Example nginx config:
```nginx
brotli on;
brotli_static on;
gzip on;
```

Using Clerk’s `<Show when="signed-in">` component in an Astro template controls UI visibility based on authentication state on the client side, while protecting a route with `clerkMiddleware()` in `src/middleware.ts` enforces access control on the server side.

The `<Show>` component is ideal for conditional rendering of UI elements like buttons or content sections depending on whether a user is signed in. It does not prevent access to the page itself — users can still navigate directly to protected pages if they know the URL, but the content remains hidden until authenticated.

In contrast, `clerkMiddleware()` provides server-side route protection by checking authentication before rendering any part of the page. If a user isn’t authenticated, middleware can redirect them away or return an unauthorized response.

Choose `<Show>` for UI-level conditional logic within pages and components where client-side behavior is acceptable. Choose `clerkMiddleware()` when you need to enforce access control at the route level — especially for sensitive data or functionality that should never be rendered without proper authentication.

A backend service manages your backend infrastructure as a cloud-based system — providing tools for databases, user authentication, and other server-side functionality. Owning that underlying infrastructure is the responsibility that frees you to focus on building your application, covering concerns such as sign-ups, persistent data storage, uploaded-asset storage, API generation, realtime communication, and monitoring.

`lang` declares what language content is in, so assistive tech, browsers, spellcheckers, and fonts handle it correctly; `translate` declares what must not be machine-translated at all (e.g. `translate="no"` on brand names, code, identifiers). They are complementary, not interchangeable: `lang` identifies the language (e.g. `<span lang="de">`), while `translate` controls inclusion in Google Translate or browser page translation, inheriting to descendants until overridden by `translate="yes"`.

Add `lang` to an inline element whenever its passage or phrase differs from the surrounding text (WCAG 3.1.2 Level AA requires it); mark the smallest correct element, e.g. `verschlimmbessern`, and use BCP 47 tags—the same tagging system as `hreflang`, such as `en-GB`, `ja-Latn`. For SEO/translation, search engines and translation tools use it to know which spans to leave alone and which to translate, and screen readers switch pronunciation. Proper names widely used in the page language don't need it. Note that since Astro v5.0, non-boolean attribute values render explicitly (`="true"`/`="false"`), so pass strings: `lang="fr"` or `lang={lang}`. Docs: https://specification.website/spec/i18n/lang-attribute/

A backend service is a cloud-based system that builds and manages your backend infrastructure for you: it provides tools for databases, user authentication, and other server-side functionality, so you focus on building the application instead of maintaining the underlying infrastructure. Managed directly, that infrastructure (database provisioning, auth, storage, APIs, monitoring) is your own responsibility. You'd consider a service — Appwrite, Firebase, Neon, Prisma Postgres, Supabase, Turso, Xata, Sentry, Scalekit — when your project has complex server-side needs: user sign-ups and authentication, persistent data or uploaded-asset storage, API generation, realtime communication, or application monitoring.

A backend service delivers all of them from one cloud-based system: it provides a single set of tools and services for managing databases, user authentication, and other server-side functionality, so authentication, storage, and monitoring come from one integrated, managed platform instead of separate self-hosted implementations — and you don't have to worry about managing the underlying infrastructure. The architectural benefit is that unified managed layer rather than stitching together and operating distinct backends, letting you focus on building the application.

    {Object.entries(languages).map(([lang, label]) => (
  • {label}
    • ))}
``` Render it on every page (e.g. in your base layout's footer), and don't use flags for languages.

Install with npm install astro.

``` The value inherits to all descendants until a child sets `translate="yes"`; the document default is translatable. Google Translate, browsers' built-in page translation, and human-translation tools honor it — `lang` does not: `lang` declares what language content is in, while `translate="no"` declares what must not be machine-translated at all. Use it identically in Astro component templates.

Astro has no built-in IP- or `Accept-Language`-based locale redirect, so there is no Astro option to disable — simply avoid adding any server, CDN, or edge logic that inspects the visitor's IP or `Accept-Language` and 302s them to `/de/` or a localized subdomain. Make the URL alone determine the content: each localized route always serves its declared language for every visitor, ship a visible language switcher on every page, optionally show a non-blocking "also available in …" banner, and persist the user's *explicit* choice in a cookie. Never silently rewrite a page's content based on the visitor's country.

Make the path alone determine the content: each localized route must render its declared language unconditionally, with no server, CDN, or edge logic rewriting output from the visitor's IP or `Accept-Language`, and no bounce to another locale. A request for `/de/about` returns German even to a US visitor, so crawlers reach every translation and shared links keep meaning what they said. Generate one route per locale and give users a visible language switcher to move between them. When extracting a locale from a path with Astro's i18n utilities, check `pathHasLocale` first to avoid `i18nNoLocaleFoundInPath` on paths that contain no locale.

The `redirects` config is declarative and build-time: a route-to-destination mapping in `astro.config.mjs` (added in 2.9.0) for known, unconditional URL changes. With no adapter in static output it emits a `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` and status codes are ignored; with SSR or a static adapter, status codes are supported — 301 for GET, 308 for other methods, customizable via `{ status, destination }`.

`Astro.redirect()` is imperative and runs per-request in a page's frontmatter — use it when the decision depends on the request (e.g. a cookie/session check). It requires on-demand rendering and must run at the page level, not in child components.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/configuration-reference/

You don't need a backend service when your project has no complex server-side needs — specifically none of: user sign-ups and authentication, persistent data storage, user-uploaded asset storage, API generation, realtime communication, or application monitoring. A site that only renders pages (static output with no server logic) works entirely within Astro, and added features can come from community integrations. Reach for a backend service only when one of those capabilities becomes a requirement.

Include the page itself in each sitemap entry's `links` array: `SitemapItem.links` "defines a list of alternate pages, including the current page," and every URL in that list must appear with its own `<loc>` entry carrying the matching `<xhtml:link>` hreflang, so each cluster member references itself.

```js
{
  url: 'https://example.com/en/page',
  links: [
    { lang: 'en', url: 'https://example.com/en/page' }, // self-reference
    { lang: 'de', url: 'https://example.com/de/seite' },
    { lang: 'fr', url: 'https://example.com/fr/page' },
  ],
}
```

Set either `lang` or `hreflang` on a `LinkItem` — when one is set you do not need the other — and repeat the same full alternate set on every URL in the cluster, including the self entry.

Give every locale its own translated `<title>` and `<meta name="description">` (plus `og:*`, `twitter:*`, JSON-LD, and `alt` strings) in your layout's `<head>`, driven by the active locale — a translated body with English metadata is half a translation and is what appears in search results and social previews. Also set the matching `lang` on `<html>` so assistive tech and crawlers know the metadata's language.

With Starlight, pass an object keyed by locale to the `title` option instead of a single string:

```js
starlight({
  title: { en: 'My Docs', 'zh-CN': '我的文档' },
  defaultLocale: 'en',
  locales: { en: { label: 'English' }, 'zh-cn': { label: '简体中文', lang: 'zh-CN' } },
})
```

Docs: https://starlight.astro.build/guides/i18n/

`og:locale` declares to social platforms which language/region a page's Open Graph card belongs to, so unfurl previews match the page's audience; set `og:locale` to the current page's locale and `og:locale:alternate` to list the other locales. Open Graph uses underscored tags such as `fr_FR`, unlike the BCP 47 tags (`fr-CA`) used elsewhere in your HTML and hreflang — that mismatch is OGP's quirk.

In Astro, emit it per page in your layout's `<head>` from the active locale:

```astro
<meta property="og:locale" content="fr_FR" />
<meta property="og:locale:alternate" content="en_US" />
```

Translate the accompanying `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:site_name`, and `og:image:alt` at the same time.

Import images from `src/` so Astro reads their metadata (`ImageMetadata`: `src`, `width`, `height`, `format`) and either render them with the `` component — it optimizes the file and infers width/height from the original aspect ratio to avoid CLS — or pass those properties yourself: ```astro --- import myDog from '../../images/pets/local-dog.jpg'; --- ``` For images destined outside HTML (API routes, custom components), use `getImage()` from `astro:assets`; it is server-only, so call it in frontmatter and pass the resulting `src` to the client. If Astro cannot read an imported file, you get the "Could not process image metadata" error — re-export the image from your editor. Note that since Astro 6, responsive styles are emitted as a hashed class plus `data-astro-fit`/`data-astro-pos` attributes rather than inline `style` values. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/images/

`hreflang` in the `<head>` tells search engines which URL to serve for which user's language and region — the signal is identical to declaring the same alternates in the XML sitemap, only the delivery mechanism changes. It makes the correct localized URL surface in regional results (e.g. the French page on `google.fr` instead of the English one).

It does not translate anything: hreflang selects the URL, while the title, meta description, Open Graph fields, and JSON-LD must still be localised themselves, or the SERP snippet and social card appear in the wrong language even though the ranking is correct. Pair head hreflang with per-locale metadata and a matching `lang` on `<html>`.

Use the ccTLD pattern: give every locale its own country-code domain, e.g. `https://example.de/`, `https://example.com/`, rather than subdomains or subdirectories. Pick this single pattern for the whole site before building, because hreflang, sitemaps, canonical tags, the language switcher, and analytics all reference those URLs — changing later requires rebuilding each with 301 redirects. ccTLD gives automatic geotargeting by TLD and the strongest perceived locality, at the highest infra cost (separate domains, certificates, DNS) and the hardest job consolidating authority across locales. Localized content still lives in per-locale directories in your project (e.g. `src/pages/` folders), with each domain serving its locale.

Give every localized URL a self-referencing canonical and a complete set of reciprocal `hreflang` alternates in its `<head>`, all pointing at the same fixed URL pattern. Each page must list itself, link back to every page that links to it (one-way links are ignored), use BCP 47 codes (`en-GB`, `pt-BR`; never region alone), and include an `x-default` entry for the fallback URL. Generate the alternate URLs with the `astro:i18n` helpers so they respect `base`, `trailingSlash`, and `build.format`:

```astro
---
import { getRelativeLocaleUrl } from 'astro:i18n';
const en = getRelativeLocaleUrl('en', 'about');
const es = getRelativeLocaleUrl('es', 'about');
---
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href={en} />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="es" href={es} />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href={en} />
```

hreflang only asserts equivalence — it never declares a page's language, which comes from content and the `lang` attribute.

Keep localization in the URL structure and file organization, not in the `slug` schema field. `slug` is reserved by Astro for entry slug generation: a legacy collection schema containing it throws `ContentSchemaContainsSlugError`, and an entry whose `slug` is not a string throws an invalid-slug error — so supply custom slugs in frontmatter instead of the schema. Organize content per locale (e.g. `src/pages/[locale]/` folders or per-language content directories) so every localized page has its own stable URL under one chosen pattern, and localise the slugs only optionally on top of that. Because slugs sit inside the URL pattern that hreflang, canonicals, and sitemans all reference, keep the pattern fixed and change slugs only with 301 redirects.

Add one `<link rel="alternate">` element per locale variant to the page `<head>`, using BCP 47 codes:

```html
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-GB" href="https://example.com/en-gb/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-US" href="https://example.com/en-us/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr-CA" href="https://example.com/fr-ca/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href="https://example.com/" />
```

Rules: every page must list itself (self-reference), links must be reciprocal — if A points to B, B must point back or both are ignored — region-only codes like `hreflang="GB"` are invalid, script subtags (`zh-Hans`, `zh-Hant`) are allowed, and `x-default` covers the URL shown when no alternate matches. Pick a single delivery method: HTML `<link>` for statically rendered pages, or the HTTP `Link` header / sitemap `<xhtml:link>` instead, never a mix.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/i18n/hreflang/

`Astro.preferredLocaleList` (added in `astro@3.5.0`) returns `string[]` of locales that are both requested by the visitor's browser and supported by your site, in preference order — so pick the first entry as the best match: ```astro --- const supported = Astro.preferredLocaleList; const locale = supported?.[0] ?? Astro.currentLocale ?? 'en'; ---

Viewing in {locale}

``` Key behaviors: `[]` means no browser language is supported (fall back to your default locale); if the browser sends no preferences, the value is your entire `i18n.locales` array, so treat that case as "no preference" rather than a match. It is only available on routes rendered on demand — never on prerendered, static pages — while `Astro.currentLocale` (from the URL) works everywhere. All locales used must exist in `i18n.locales` with matching `src/pages/` directories, or `MissingLocale` is thrown. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/api-reference/

When using Astro's `<ClientRouter />` with forms, the default behavior for `POST` methods is to submit as `multipart/form-data`, but if you want browser-like behavior, you must explicitly set `enctype="application/x-www-form-urlencoded"` on your form. If this isn't specified and your form uses `method="POST"`, it will send a POST request with the default encoding.

If your form is submitting to a new URL using view transitions and unexpectedly becomes a POST instead of GET, ensure that:
1. The form's method is explicitly set as `GET` if you want a GET request.
2. If using `POST`, add `enctype="application/x-www-form-urlencoded"` for standard behavior.

Example:

```astro
<form action="/contact" method="GET">
  <!-- or -->
<form action="/contact" method="POST" enctype="application/x-www-form-urlencoded">
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/view-transitions/#transitions-with-forms

Preview is explicitly not designed for production use. `astro.config.mjs` configures the project itself (e.g. `site`, `base`, `trailingSlash`), not which task runs.

The query fails: an element cannot query itself, so `@container` rules targeting the element you placed `container-type` on will not style it. Set `container-type: inline-size` (plus optional `container-name`) on an ancestor wrapper instead, and write `@container` rules that apply to that container's descendants. Advertise the hub with two link relations: `rel="hub"` naming the hub that will distribute your topic, and `rel="self"` naming the topic's canonical URL. Both can travel as HTTP `Link` headers or as elements inside the document or feed (e.g. `<link>` tags in your layout's `<head>`); subscribers check `Link` headers first and fall back to embedded elements. Note that `rel="hub"` is only an advertisement — delivery happens only when the hub is notified of a change and subscribers renew their lease.

Store content and data entries in **separate collections by type**: split them into one collection for content entries and another configured with `type: 'data'` for data entries. Mixing them in a single legacy collection raises **MixedContentDataCollectionError**: `COLLECTION_NAME contains a mix of content and data entries. All entries must be of the same type.` A related error, `ContentCollectionTypeMismatchError`, appears when entries don't match the configured type — collections are `type: 'content'` by default, so data collections must opt in with `type: 'data'` in the collection config.

Add two `<meta name="theme-color">` tags to your page head, one per colour scheme, using the `media` attribute so the browser picks the value matching the user's current scheme:

```html
<meta name="theme-color" content="#ffffff" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" />
<meta name="theme-color" content="#0b1020" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" />
```

Browsers select whichever tag's media query matches; a single tag without `media` is used in every mode. Pick colours matching the edges of your page (the strip sits flush against your `<body>` background). For an installed PWA, also set `theme_color` in the web app manifest — it's used once at install/launch, while the meta tag is consulted on every page load.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/foundations/theme-color/

Ship a pair of `theme-color` meta tags with `media` queries so the browser always follows the OS colour scheme:

```html
<meta name="theme-color" content="#ffffff" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" />
<meta name="theme-color" content="#0b1020" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" />
```

Browsers pick the tag whose `media` query matches the user's current scheme, so the address bar, status bar, and task-switcher tint track system light/dark settings automatically. Note that an installed PWA's manifest `theme_color` is only used at install/launch — the meta tag is what stays in sync on every page load, so matching both avoids a visible jump.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/foundations/theme-color/

Neon is a fully managed serverless Postgres database (autoscaling, branching, bottomless storage); you connect with `@neondatabase/serverless` using a `NEON_DATABASE_URL` environment variable, and it requires an Astro project with on-demand rendering (SSR) enabled. The `atom:link rel="self"` element makes the feed self-identifying: it carries the feed's own canonical subscription URL inside the feed document, so the feed stays portable — if it is mirrored, cached, or forwarded by a reader, aggregators can still locate the canonical subscription URL instead of guessing. It complements `<link rel="alternate">` in your page `<head>` (which handles discovery from your site to the feed): this element handles identification within the feed itself. Declare the Atom namespace `xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom"` on the `<rss>` root and ship the self-link in `<channel>`.

Relative paths are unsupported in the `content` field (added in `astro@1.6.14`): only images and links with full URL paths work, so relative `src`/`href` values break in feed readers, which resolve them against the feed's URL rather than your page. Fix this in your `src/pages/rss.xml.js` endpoint — add logic that rewrites relative image and internal-link paths to absolute URLs based on `site`, and remove elements that exist only for site styling or interaction. Render content-collection bodies with `markdown-it` and sanitize via `sanitize-html` (extend `allowedTags` with `img`); for glob-imported Markdown use `compiledContent()` (not supported for MDX).

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/recipes/rss/

const isProd = import.meta.env.PUBLIC_ENV === 'production';

{isProd && <meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/og.png" />}

Set `site` in your Astro config, then build the canonical from `Astro.url.pathname`, which contains no query string:

```astro
---
const canonicalURL = new URL(Astro.url.pathname, Astro.site);
---
<link rel="canonical" href={canonicalURL} />
```

`Astro.site` supplies the production origin, so the result is the absolute URL (scheme + host + path) that canonical tags require, while parameters such as `?utm_source=newsletter` or `?sort=date` are dropped because only `pathname` is used. ---
<meta name="description" content={description} />
```

Two pages with the same description send a duplicate-content signal, and a missing description forces search engines to invent a snippet from the page body.

In a Starlight project, set the `titleDelimiter` option (type `string`, default `'|'`) in the `starlight` integration configuration in `astro.config.mjs` — it controls the separator between page title and site title in every page's `<title>`, which is what appears on browser tabs, so titles render as "Page Title | Site Title" by default and with your chosen character otherwise. In a plain Astro site, compose the title yourself in `<head>`: page-specific text first, site name second, separated by a delimiter such as `·`, `—`, or `|` (e.g. `Setting up CSP · The Website Specification`). Keep one unique title per page, around 50–60 characters.

Put the viewport meta tag in `<head>`:

```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
```

`width=device-width` makes mobile browsers render at the device's real width instead of the legacy 980-pixel desktop canvas, and `initial-scale=1` sets 1:1 zoom, so responsive CSS like `@media (max-width: 600px)` works as designed. Never add `user-scalable=no` or `maximum-scale=1` — disabling pinch zoom fails WCAG 1.4.4. For images, use `<Image />` or `<Picture />` from `astro:assets` with a `layout` prop so `srcset`, `sizes`, and resizing styles are generated automatically (images in `public/` are never optimized).
