The modern `<!doctype html>` declares no HTML version — its only job is to switch the browser into standards mode, whereas legacy HTML 4.01 and XHTML doctypes pointed at a DTD and were read as declaring a document version. Both are valid, but some legacy doctypes trigger a "limited-quirks" mode you should never need. In your Astro pages, put `<!doctype html>` on line one (it is case-insensitive) with no whitespace, comments, or XML prolog before it, and replace any legacy doctype. Modern elements like `<section>` parse with or without a doctype; the doctype only decides rendering mode — absent or malformed means quirks mode and broken CSS.

For actions, throw an `ActionError` from the `handler()` instead of returning `undefined`: import it from `astro:actions` and pass a human-readable `code` (e.g. `"NOT_FOUND"`, `"UNAUTHORIZED"`) plus an optional `message`. This sets the HTTP status (404, 401) on the request and surfaces the error as `error` on the action result, so callers can branch on `error.code`:

```ts
import { defineAction, ActionError } from "astro:actions";
throw new ActionError({ code: "UNAUTHORIZED", message: "User must be logged in." });
```

Plain endpoints must return a `Response` (or a `Promise` resolving to one); returning anything else throws `EndpointDidNotReturnAResponse`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/

`src/pages/api/[id].json.js` is a dynamic endpoint: the bracketed `[id]` enables the same dynamic routing as pages, so you export `getStaticPaths()` to generate concrete routes at build time (e.g. `/api/0.json` … `/api/3.json`) and read the value from `params.id` inside `GET`. It otherwise behaves like any other endpoint — `GET` receives a context with `params`/`request` and must return a `Response`. The difference from a plain `data.json.ts` file is that the extension in the filename survives the build: the `.js`/`.ts` extension is stripped, so `[id].json.js` keeps `.json` as the served extension. Endpoints whose URLs include a file extension are only accessible without a trailing slash.

Configure i18n routing with an `i18n` config whose `locales` array lists your supported languages, providing `codes` in the same pattern browsers use in the `Accept-Language` header — that is what makes matching work. Then, in pages rendered on demand, read `Astro.preferredLocale` (the best single match between `Accept-Language` and your `locales`, `undefined` if none) or `Astro.preferredLocaleList` (all locales both the browser requested and the site supports, `[]` on no match) and redirect or render accordingly. All pages, including prerendered ones, have `Astro.currentLocale`, but browser-language detection itself is only available on on-demand rendered pages.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/internationalization/

`Astro.preferredLocale` is computed from the browser's `Accept-Language` header matched against your `i18n.locales` array — it is the visitor's best-fit language, is `undefined` if no match exists, and is only available on routes rendered on demand, never on prerendered static pages. `Astro.currentLocale` is computed from the current URL using your `locales` syntax (defaulting to `i18n.defaultLocale` when the URL has no `/[locale]/` prefix) and is available on every page. Use `preferredLocale` on server-rendered routes to pick or redirect to a visitor's language; use `currentLocale` to render links and UI in the language the URL already selects, e.g. `getRelativeLocaleUrl(Astro.currentLocale ?? 'en', 'about')`.

Serve proper cache headers; that is the whole fix. Astro's prefetch uses `<link rel="prefetch">` when supported and falls back to `fetch()` otherwise. Firefox supports `<link rel="prefetch">` but errors with `NS_BINDING_ABORTED` unless the response carries an explicit `Cache-Control` or `Expires` header; with a valid `ETag`, the response is still re-used on navigation despite the error, but with no cache headers at all the prefetch simply fails. Safari has no `<link rel="prefetch">` support, so it always falls back to `fetch()`, which likewise requires `Cache-Control`, `Expires`, or `ETag` — and `ETag` does not work in Safari private windows. For static or prerendered pages, `ETag` is usually set automatically by your deployment platform; for SSR pages, set the cache headers yourself.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/prefetch/

Mutate the existing `Headers` instance rather than replacing it. Assigning a new `Headers` to `Astro.response.headers` throws `AstroResponseHeadersReassigned` — individual headers may be added and removed, but the object itself must not be swapped out. `Astro.response` is a `ResponseInit` whose `headers` field is `readonly` (`ResponseInit & { readonly headers: Headers }`), so set values directly:

```astro
---
Astro.response.headers.set('Set-Cookie', 'a=b; Path=/;');
---
```

Also note that headers, cookies, and status can only be changed in page components before the response is sent; afterwards you get `ResponseSentError`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/astro-response-headers-reassigned/

Emit a single comma-separated `Link` response header advertising each machine-readable surface, using only registered IANA relation types:

```http
Link: </llms.txt>; rel="describedby"; type="text/markdown"; title="Site index for LLMs",
      </.well-known/api-catalog>; rel="api-catalog"; type="application/linkset+json",
      </sitemap-index.xml>; rel="sitemap"; type="application/xml",
      </rss.xml>; rel="alternate"; type="application/rss+xml"
```

Sending several `Link` headers instead is equally valid per RFC 8288 §3. The header travels with every response, so agents that never parse your HTML still discover everything, and a CDN can cache alternative representations from it. Attach it at the host level — e.g. `vercel.json` on Vercel can attach headers to HTTP responses — and use the HTML `<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml">` tag for browser-side RSS autodiscovery. Choose `rel` values from the IANA registry: `describedby` for llms.txt, `api-catalog` (RFC 9727), `sitemap`, `alternate`.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/agent-readiness/link-headers/

Use a two-letter code like `en`, a region variant like `en-GB` or `pt-BR` when it changes spelling or pronunciation, `lang` on child elements for inline foreign text, and pair `dir="rtl"` with `lang` for Arabic or Hebrew. In Astro, set it on the root element of your layout.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/foundations/html-lang/

The level used to filter messages is `"info"`.

Since the `logger.config` in `astro.config.mjs` omits the `config` key, the custom logger implementation receives a default configuration object with only `{}` (an empty object) passed as its argument. The destructuring assignment in the function signature `function orgLogger({ level } = { level: 'info' })` provides `"info"` as the fallback value for `level` when it is not present or undefined in the received config.

This behavior aligns with JavaScript’s default parameter syntax, where the right-hand side of the assignment is evaluated only if the argument is missing or explicitly passed as `undefined`. In this case, since no `config.level` was provided, the fallback `{ level: 'info' }` applies.

The `memoryCache` provider is a runtime (in-memory) provider, not a CDN provider. It implements `onRequest()` for in-process caching and does not support path-based invalidation via `cache.invalidate({ path })` — it only supports tag-based invalidation. Path-based invalidation works only with CDN providers (Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare) that translate it to tag purges. Use tags instead: `cache.invalidate({ tags: ['products'] })`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/cache-provider-reference/

Import `global.css` with an ESM import in the component frontmatter; your local `<style>` tags won't conflict because Astro scopes them automatically by default. Scoped rules are compiled to selectors like `h1[data-astro-cid-hhnqfkh6]`, so they only apply to HTML written inside that same component and don't leak. Specificity is preserved, so component styles work consistently alongside global CSS files. Opt out of scoping only when you intentionally want global rules, with `<style is:global>` or the `:global()` selector.

```
---
import '../styles/utils.css';
---
<style>h1 { color: red; }</style>
```

Configure the font in `astro.config` with a `cssVariable`, then import `global.css` once in your shared layout and apply that variable there — every page using the layout gets the font, while component `<style>` tags stay scoped and can't leak or conflict.

```
---
import { Font } from "astro:assets";
import "../styles/global.css";
---
<html>
  <head><Font cssVariable="--font-roboto" /></head>
  <body><slot /></body>
</html>
```

In `global.css`, e.g. `body { font-family: var(--font-roboto); }` (Tailwind 4: `@theme inline { --font-sans: var(--font-roboto); }`). Because it's driven by a CSS variable, individual pages/components can override it locally.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/fonts/

A `<style>` rule referencing an undefined variable simply won't take effect — the style is only applied when the variable is actually available on the page. Avoid this by defining the value in your component frontmatter and passing it into the style with `define:vars`, which exposes it as a CSS custom property:

```
---
const skillColor = "crimson";
const fontWeight = "bold";
---
<style define:vars={{ skillColor, fontWeight }}>
  .skill { color: var(--skillColor); font-weight: var(--fontWeight); }
</style>
```

Alternatively, ensure the variable is defined elsewhere on the page (e.g. in a global stylesheet), since Astro styles can reference any CSS variable available on the page.

Per-route `cache.set()` calls merge with config-level route rules, so `cache.set({ maxAge: 600 })` on a route matched by `{ maxAge: 3600, tags: ['products'] }` overrides the config `maxAge` to 600 seconds while the rule's other defaults are extended into the merged cache options. Route code can override or extend the defaults set in config on a per-request basis; for example, individual pages can call `cache.set()` to customize or disable caching as needed. To opt a request out of caching entirely when a matched route rule would otherwise cache it, call `cache.set(false)`.

The practical benefit is that cached responses are shared across all edge nodes instead of being confined to a single one, so cache hits are served straight from the CDN regardless of which node receives the request. This reduces function invocations compared to a standard edge cache. The `cacheNetlify()` provider enables this by setting `Netlify-CDN-Cache-Control` and `Netlify-Cache-Tag` headers via Netlify's durable cache, and it supports both tag-based and path-based invalidation.

Choose NOT to use `cacheVercel()` when you need hard, immediate invalidation: its tag invalidation is a soft invalidation, where cached responses are only marked as stale and revalidated in the background using stale-while-revalidate. After you invalidate, stale responses can still be served while revalidation runs. If invalidated content must stop being served right away, this provider's behavior is insufficient. Also note that during the experimental phase these providers must be manually enabled.

The script will be included only **once** in the final HTML. Astro deduplicates by bundling all `<script>` tags from the same component and including the bundled script a single time per page, regardless of how many times the component appears.

Duplication causes problems when the inline script defines global functions, variables, or registers custom elements — each instance re-executes the code, leading to "already defined" errors or multiple event listeners on the same elements. Instead, remove `is:inline` to let Astro process and deduplicate the script, then use `document.querySelectorAll()` to target all component instances from a single script execution. For per-instance logic, define a custom element (`customElements.define`) whose `connectedCallback` runs once per instance while the class definition remains deduplicated.

The `entrypoint` property in a session driver config defines the runtime entrypoint for the driver implementation. It must be a string or URL pointing to the module that exports the `SessionDriver` implementation (with `setItem`, `getItem`, `removeItem` methods). In the config function, it's typically set using `new URL('./runtime.js', import.meta.url)` to reference a local runtime file, or a string like `"unstorage/drivers/redis"` for Unstorage drivers. The entrypoint is required and was added in `astro@6.0.0`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/session-driver-reference/

Avoid the built-in `memory` driver when running multiple server instances (e.g., scaled deployments, serverless functions, or clustered environments) because in-memory storage is not shared across instances. Sessions would be lost or inconsistent between requests hitting different instances. Use a distributed driver like Redis instead.

Example scenario: A production Astro site deployed to a container orchestrator (Kubernetes, ECS) with 3 replicas behind a load balancer. User logs in on replica A, but next request routes to replica B which has no session data — user appears logged out.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/session-driver-reference/

A `<script>` with no attributes (only `src` allowed) is processed: TypeScript support, import bundling of local files and npm packages, automatic `type="module"`, deduplication to one inclusion per page even if the component repeats, and automatic inlining when small. With `is:inline`, the tag is emitted into the final HTML exactly as authored—no TypeScript, no import resolution, no bundling, and no deduplication, so it appears once per component instance. Note `is:inline` is implied by any attribute other than `src`. Opt out of processing when loading a script from `public/` or a remote server, or when you need the literal output preserved:

```astro
<script is:inline src="https://my-analytics.com/script.js"></script>
```

Because Astro only processes `<script>` tags that have no attributes other than `src`; any other attribute implicitly applies `is:inline`, opting the tag out of processing entirely. Your `data-foo` marks the script as inline, so it is rendered verbatim: no TypeScript transpilation, no import resolution or bundling, and no deduplication. Keep scripts processed by leaving them bare (or with only `src`), and pass runtime values through a `data-*` attribute on a surrounding element instead of onto the `<script>` itself, reading them in the processed script via `dataset`.

Include it with the `is:inline` directive: scripts living outside your project's `src/` folder (in `public/` or on a CDN) must skip Astro's processing, bundling, and optimizations.

```astro
<!-- absolute path to a script at `public/my-script.js` -->
<script is:inline src="/my-script.js"></script>
<!-- full URL to a script on a remote server -->
<script is:inline src="https://my-analytics.com/script.js"></script>
```

The tag is rendered into the final HTML exactly as written—no transformation, no import resolution, and no deduplication. A third-party analytics snippet doesn't need bundling; it just needs to load as-is.

The script will appear **once** in the final HTML. Astro deduplicates scripts: when a component containing a `<script>` tag (without attributes other than `src`) is used multiple times on a page, Astro bundles the script and includes it only once per page.

`memoryCache()` is a **runtime provider** that intercepts requests and stores responses in-process (in memory) — it serves hits from your server instance and adds an `X-Astro-Cache` header, making it suitable only for single-instance deployments. Adapter CDN providers like `cacheNetlify()` are **CDN providers**: rather than storing responses in memory, they translate cache directives into platform headers (`Netlify-CDN-Cache-Control`, `Netlify-Cache-Tag`) and push them to the host's edge network, so cache hits are served straight from the CDN without invoking your server function. The internal CDN headers are stripped before the response reaches the client. Netlify additionally uses durable cache shared across all edge nodes.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/caching/

Use `routeRules` in `astro.config.mjs` to set declarative cache defaults for route groups, and `context.cache.set()` in an API route when a single request needs different or conditional options (custom `maxAge`/`tags`, or `cache.set(false)` to opt out). When both are present for the same route, they merge: per-route `cache.set()` calls can override or extend the values set by the matched config rule.

Options may be missing because no `cache.provider` is configured or the app is running in dev mode—`context.cache.enabled` is `false` in both cases, `cache.set()` and `cache.options` only warn, and accumulated options only exist after a `cache.set()` call in that request; `context.cache` itself is typed `object | undefined`. Verify with `if (context.cache.enabled)` before reading `cache.options`, configure `cache: { provider: memoryCache() }`, and build + preview to test outside dev.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/configuration-reference/

You cannot configure invalidation declaratively via `routeRules`. Route rules only set caching options (`maxAge`, `swr`, `tags`) for matched routes; a `tags` value marks responses for later invalidation but does not purge entries. The only documented syntax for tag-based invalidation is runtime: `await context.cache.invalidate({ tags: ['data'] })` (path invalidation is exact-match only).

This design allows developers to opt out of processing by simply adding an attribute, and ensures external scripts (which often need specific attributes) are not accidentally bundled or transpiled. The behavior changed from Astro v0.x where `hoist` was required to opt in; now processing is opt-out by attribute presence.

`memoryCache()` is a runtime provider: responses are stored in-process in an LRU map inside your server instance (default `max: 1000` entries, evicting least-recently-used), so hits are served from that process's memory — it's explicitly suited only to single-instance deployments, and adds an `X-Astro-Cache: HIT`/`MISS`/`STALE` header for observability.

If you need cache entries to survive deployments, Cloudflare's Workers Cache is enabled with default settings, which can drop the cache on a new version unless you reconfigure it. Also, CDN caching only pays off across multiple edge nodes; `memoryCache()` is the documented choice for single-instance deployments where responses can be held in-process.

Use `pathHasLocale()` whenever you need to know whether an arbitrary path contains one of your configured locales — especially as a guard before calling an i18n utility that reads a locale from a URL path, which otherwise throws `i18nNoLocaleFoundInPath`. It checks against your `i18n.locales` configuration (including custom path forms like `italiano`), so it replaces hand-parsing path segments and maintaining your own duplicate list of locale prefixes:

```
import { pathHasLocale } from "astro:i18n";
pathHasLocale('/es/blog/'); // true
pathHasLocale("it-VT");     // false (code, not the configured path)
```

`pathHasLocale()` simply returns `false` — it never throws for paths lacking a locale. That's exactly why it exists: call it first to guard i18n utilities that extract a locale from a path, since using such a utility on a locale-less path otherwise throws the `i18nNoLocaleFoundInPath` error ("You tried to use an i18n utility on a path that doesn't contain any locale"). Note it only detects *configured* locales: `pathHasLocale("it-VT")` returns `false` when only `{ path: "italiano", codes: ["it-VT", "it"] }` is configured, because the URL path would need to be `italiano`.

The issue is that payloads sent via `toolbar.send()` must be serializable, but JavaScript class instances are not automatically serializable. The Dev Toolbar uses structured cloning or JSON serialization to transmit data between client and server, which fails with class instances.

The `toolbar` object's `send()` method accepts any value that can be serialized using the [structured clone algorithm](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/structuredClone), such as primitives, arrays, plain objects, and certain built-in types like `Date`, `Map`, `Set`. Class instances (e.g., `{ ... }` from a class constructor) cannot be passed directly.

To fix this, convert your class instance to a plain object before sending:

```js
toolbar.send('server-message', obj.toJSON ? obj.toJSON() : Object.assign({}, obj));
```

Disabling streaming means the browser no longer receives HTML chunk-by-chunk as components finish rendering. Without it, rendering effectively waits — as with `await`ed fetches in frontmatter, where all HTML delivery is held up until every fetch resolves — so first content arrives later and blocking data fetches hurt perceived performance more. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/image-service-reference/

`injectRoute()` is a callback on the `astro:config:setup` hook, typed `({ pattern: string; entrypoint: string | URL; prerender?: boolean }) => void`, for injecting `.astro` pages or `.js`/`.ts` route handlers:

```js
injectRoute({
  pattern: '/subfolder/[dynamic]',
  entrypoint: './src/dynamic-page.astro',
  prerender: false,
});
```

- `pattern` is the output path and uses Astro's filepath syntax for dynamic routes (`/foo/[bar]`, `/foo/[...bar]`); no file extension.
- `entrypoint` is a bare module specifier; since `astro@5.0.0` it may also be a `URL`, e.g. `new URL('./dashboard.astro', import.meta.url)`.
- `prerender` is only a fallback for when Astro can't detect your `prerender` export.

For a published package, reference the entrypoint by package name (`'@fancy/dashboard/dashboard.astro'`) and expose it via `package.json` `"exports"`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/integrations-reference/

Nothing — it is valid and expected. `astro:config:done` is typed `(options: {...}) => void | Promise<void>`, so it returns no value and an `undefined` return is ignored; do your work through the hook's options (`config`, `setAdapter()`, `injectTypes()`, `buildOutput`, `logger`) rather than through a return value.

Use `client:only` when a component must not render HTML on the server, such as when it depends on client-specific APIs or behavior that isn't available during SSR. Unlike `client:load`, which renders static HTML on the server before hydrating on the client, `client:only` skips server rendering entirely and only mounts the component in the browser.

Example:
```astro
<ClientComponent client:only="react" />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/#clientonly

With `fallbackType: "redirect"` (default), the browser navigates to the fallback locale's URL, changing the address bar. With `fallbackType: "rewrite"`, Astro renders the fallback page's content at the originally requested URL without redirecting. For example, if `fr` falls back to `es` and `/fr/about` doesn't exist, "redirect" sends the user to `/es/about`, while "rewrite" shows the English content at `/fr/about`.

Avoid using `refreshContent()` outside the `astro:server:setup` hook during development. It is designed specifically for `astro dev` to trigger content layer updates (e.g., from CMS webhooks or websockets). It will not work in production builds or static generation contexts where there is no running dev server to receive the refresh signal.

```ts
return notes
  .filter((note) => note.readPermission === 'guest')
  .map((note) => ({
    params: { slug: getNoteSlug(note) },
    props: { noteId: note.id },
  }));
```

`SSRManifest.key` (type `Promise<CryptoKey>`, added in `astro@4.13.4`) is the cryptographic key used for encrypting server island props, protecting sensitive data from accidental exposure. Astro generates a new random key on each build and embeds it in the server bundle; in the serialized manifest handed to `astro:build:ssr`, the same property is a `string`. If your frontend (encrypting) and backend (decrypting) can fall out of sync — rolling deployments, multi-region hosting, CDN-cached pages — run `astro create-key` and set the resulting `ASTRO_KEY` environment variable so the same key is reused at build time.

Nothing — `astro:build:ssr` is typed as `(options) => void | Promise<void>`, so it has no return value for Astro to consume; the hook only hands you `manifest` (a `SerializedSSRManifest`), `middlewareEntryPoint`, and `logger`. There is also no `entryPoints` array involved: it was always empty after the Astro 5 `functionPerRoute` deprecation and was removed entirely in Astro 6.

In `SSRComponentMetadata.propagation` (`'none' | 'self' | 'in-tree'`), `self` means this component itself appends the head content, while `in-tree` means another component within this component's dependency tree appends the head content — in both cases the Astro runtime may need to wait for the component. `none` means the component does not propagate head content. The companion `containsHead: boolean` states whether the component contains head content. These entries are exposed as `SSRManifest.componentMetadata`, a `Map<string, SSRComponentMetadata>` added in `astro@2.1.7`.

`astro:build:start` runs after `astro:config:done` but before the production build begins, and exists to set up global objects or clients needed during the build and to extend build configuration options in the adapter API. It receives `logger` and `setPrerenderer()` (added in `astro@6.0.0`): a callback accepting either an `AstroPrerenderer` object directly, or a factory that receives the default prerenderer and returns a wrapped/custom one, letting adapters supply their own prerendering logic.

They fire in sequence during dev only: `astro:server:setup` runs just after Vite creates the server but before `listen()` — use it to mutate the `ViteDevServer`, add middleware with `server.middlewares.use()`, access the dev `toolbar` helpers, or call `refreshContent()`. `astro:server:start` runs just after `listen()` and receives `address: AddressInfo` (address, family, port) for working with the network address. If you use middleware, prefer `astro:server:setup`; then use `astro:server:done` to clean up anything started in either hook.

Use the `injectScript()` callback provided by the `astro:config:setup` hook in your integration, with the `"page-ssr"` stage: `injectScript('page-ssr', 'import "your-script.js";')`. This injects your content as a separate module imported in the frontmatter of every Astro page component, so it executes only on the server during rendering. Because the script is imported, the `Astro` global is not available inside it, and it runs once when the `import` is first evaluated. The other stages (`"head-inline"`, `"before-hydration"`, `"page"`) produce client-side output and would not be server-only.

`validateOptions()` is an optional hook for both local and external services (added in `astro@2.1.4`) that validates and augments the options the user passed to `<Image />`, `<Picture />`, or `getImage()`, returning the corrected `ImageTransform`. It receives `(options, imageConfig, logger)`; the `logger` parameter was added in Astro v7.3.0, so you can warn about invalid options, e.g. clamp an oversized width and call `logger.warn(...)` while falling back to `imageConfig.service.config.maxWidth`. It's the standard place for setting defaults or enforcing required parameters before `getURL()`/`transform()` run.

Through `getURL()`. In dev mode and on-demand rendering, `<Image />` and `getImage()` pass their options to `getURL()`, which serializes them into an endpoint URL (e.g. `/_image?href=...&w=...`), and the endpoint then calls `parseURL()` to recover the properties and hands them to `transform()`. At build time for static sites and prerendered routes, `getURL()` is unused: `transform()` is called directly with the options, and output files land in `dist/_astro` named by a hash of `propertiesToHash` (defaults to `['src', 'width', 'height', 'format', 'quality']`).

Implement all three local-service hooks: `transform()`, `getURL()`, and `parseURL()`. At build time for static sites and pre-rendered routes, `<Image />` and `getImage()` call `transform()` directly and emit assets to `dist/_astro`, hashing the properties in `propertiesToHash` (defaults to `['src','width','height','format','quality']`) — add any extra image-changing options there. In dev mode and on-demand rendering, `getURL()` returns an endpoint URL (your own, or the built-in `/_image`), and the endpoint calls `parseURL()` to decode the URL, then passes the result to `transform()`. External services only need `getURL()` returning the final image URL.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/image-service-reference/

For **external** services, `getURL()` returns the final image URL — the `src` of the output ``; the remote server (e.g. a CDN) does the downloading and transformation itself. For **local** services, `getURL()` returns the URL of the transformation endpoint (your own, or the built-in `/_image`) used only in dev mode and for on-demand rendering; it is **unused during build**, where ``/`getImage()` call `transform()` directly. The local endpoint then calls `parseURL()` and passes the result to `transform()`. Both hook types receive `options`, `imageConfig`, and (since v7.3.0) `logger`. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/image-service-reference/

The `client:only` directive requires an explicit renderer name because it skips server-side rendering entirely. Astro needs to know which framework to use for client-side hydration and loading, since no server render occurs to infer this automatically.

In contrast, `client:load` and other directives first render the component on the server using Astro's built-in renderer (e.g., React or Vue), so Astro can detect the correct framework from the rendered output. This allows it to avoid requiring an explicit renderer name for hydration.

Example:
```astro
<!-- Requires explicit renderer -->
<SomeReactComponent client:only="react" />

<!-- Does not require explicit renderer -->
<SomeReactComponent client:load />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/#clientonly

`listFonts()` is an optional callback of type `() => Awaitable<string[] | undefined>` (default `undefined`) that returns the list of available font names from the provider. It is useful for exposing the families a provider can serve once data is loaded — for example the private-registry example returns `Object.keys(data)` after `init()` fetched the registry, and a unifont wrapper forwards to `initializedProvider.listFonts?.()`.

To retrieve all entries from a live collection named `products` that are marked as featured, use the `getLiveCollection()` function with a filter object. The filter object should match the shape expected by your collection’s loader.

Example:

```astro
---
import { getLiveCollection } from 'astro:content';

const { entries: featuredProducts } = await getLiveCollection('products', { featured: true });
---
```

This queries only the `products` entries where the `featured` field is set to `true`. Ensure your live loader supports this filtering mechanism.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-content/#getlivecollection

You can use the `getEntries()` function to retrieve multiple related posts by passing an array of objects with the collection name and entry IDs. This is commonly used when a blog post references other posts via a `relatedPosts` field.

In your Astro component, after fetching the main post using `getEntry()`, you can call `getEntries()` with the array of referenced entries to access their data and body properties.

Example:

```astro
---
import { getEntry, getEntries } from 'astro:content';

const post = await getEntry('blog', 'my-post');
const relatedPosts = await getEntries(post.data.relatedPosts);
---
```

This allows you to fetch all related posts referenced in the `data.relatedPosts` array of your main blog post.

```ts

```

In on-demand rendering with Flotiq, `blogpostList.data?.[0]` being falsy means no matching blog post exists for the requested slug, so returning `Astro.redirect('/404')` sends users to a 404 page instead of rendering an empty or broken document. In on-demand rendering mode (Astro 7), a page can return a `Response` directly, and the Astro API that enables this is `Astro.redirect(path, status?)`, which creates a redirect response. The pattern matches the on-demand example where missing data triggers a redirect to a fallback route.

A page generated via `getStaticPaths` is prerendered at build time into a static HTML file, so if the Flotiq object is deleted after build, requests still serve that stale static page until the site is rebuilt. By contrast, an on-demand page with `Astro.params` (rendered with `prerender = false` or `output: 'server'`) fetches data at request time and can detect the missing object, then return an appropriate `Response` (e.g. 404 or redirect), reflecting the current CMS state.

To use a custom font provider, export a function that returns a `FontProvider` object (optionally accepting configuration). The provider requires `name` (unique identifier) and `async resolveFont(options)` (returns font face data or `undefined`). Optional fields include `config` (serializable), `async init(context)` for setup (with `context.storage` and `context.root`), and `async listFonts()` to return available font names. When wrapping a third-party unifont provider, store the initialized instance in `init()` and delegate `resolveFont`/`listFonts` to it.

For a local variable font, set the `weight` property of the variant to a string range (e.g. `"100 900"`) instead of a single number. In the local provider’s `variants` array, each variant specifies that range along with `style` and `src`. For example:
```js
variants: [{
  weight: "100 900",
  style: "normal",
  src: ["./src/assets/fonts/InterVariable.woff2"]
}]
```
If the weight/style cannot be inferred from the file, set them manually; this is the local provider configuration for variable fonts in Astro 7.

`listFonts()` is an optional asynchronous callback on a `FontProvider` that returns an array of available font names (or `undefined`). To implement it, delegate to the underlying provider’s `listFonts()` after initialization (e.g. `return await initializedProvider?.listFonts?.()`) or return a fixed list for a static source. It is called programmatically to enumerate available fonts and remains optional in Astro 7.

In Astro 7, `import.meta.env.PUBLIC_COSMIC_BUCKET_SLUG` is used for environment variables that are exposed to the client-side bundle, while `process.env.COSMIC_BUCKET_SLUG` refers to server-side environment variables that are not exposed to the client.

Astro requires public environment variables—those prefixed with `PUBLIC_`—to be accessible in client-side code. This ensures secure handling of API keys and other sensitive data by preventing accidental exposure of private keys in the frontend bundle. For example, when fetching data from Cosmic using the SDK, you must use `import.meta.env.PUBLIC_COSMIC_BUCKET_SLUG` because it's accessed within a client context.

For server-side operations like generating static paths or prerendering pages, you can access non-prefixed environment variables such as `process.env.COSMIC_BUCKET_SLUG`, but they are not available in the browser. Using `import.meta.env.PUBLIC_` ensures that your configuration works correctly across both environments and adheres to Astro’s security model.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/environment-variables/

You cannot directly import `trailingSlash` from `astro:config/client` in a client-side JavaScript file because it's a server-side configuration value. The `astro:config/client` module is only available during the build process and is not accessible at runtime in the browser.

If you need to check or use the trailing slash behavior in your frontend code, you should manually handle this logic based on your Astro configuration settings. For example, if you're using a base URL with a trailing slash, you can ensure consistency by appending it explicitly when needed:

```javascript
const baseUrl = import.meta.env.BASE_URL;
const hasTrailingSlash = baseUrl.endsWith('/');
```

This approach allows you to manage the behavior manually in client-side code without relying on server-specific configuration imports.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-config/

Server islands embed encrypted props using a key that regenerates on each build by default, forcing re-renders. Setting a stable `ASTRO_KEY` allows the encrypted props to be decrypted across builds, enabling incremental caching to reuse previously rendered pages. Changing the key invalidates cached islands, ensuring embedded content stays decryptable.
Run `astro build --force` to ignore the incremental cache and re-render every page. Astro will still write a fresh cache for subsequent builds.

To implement RTL support in an Astro site, set the `dir` attribute to `"rtl"` on the `<html>` tag for RTL locales. Use `lang` and `dir` together, as direction is independent of language. For example:

```astro
<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
```

For user-generated content, use `dir="auto"` so the browser detects direction from the first strong character. Avoid hard-coding physical CSS properties like `left` or `right`; instead, use CSS logical properties such as `margin-inline-start` and `padding-block-end`. This ensures layouts mirror correctly without breaking the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/i18n/rtl-support/

Avoid experimental flags in production because experimental features are not guaranteed to be stable and may include breaking changes even in small `patch` releases while the feature is actively developed. Enabling a flag means your project can break on any update, and the experimental feature documentation is only updated for the current released version, so older configs may drift from reality. To mitigate risk, update Astro frequently and watch the Astro changelog for changes needed in your project code. Note that flags are routinely removed across major versions as features stabilize: `env`, `serverIslands`, `contentLayer`, and others in v5; `csp`, `fonts`, `liveContentCollections`, `preserveScriptOrder`, `staticImportMetaEnv`, `headingIdCompat`, `failOnPrerenderConflict` in v6 — so remove obsolete flags when upgrading.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/experimental-flags/

Render your core content and navigation as plain HTML in the initial response and treat every script as an enhancement layered on top. Fallback fonts cause layout shifts when they differ significantly in metrics (ascent, descent, line height) from the primary font, causing text to reflow when the primary font loads. `optimizedFallbacks: true` (default) mitigates this by generating optimized fallback fonts using font metrics that match the primary font's dimensions, reducing visual disruption when the generic font family fallback is shown temporarily.

Set `image.responsiveStyles: true` in your Astro config (default is `false`; added in `astro@5.10.0`). These global styles are wrapped in the `:where()` pseudo-class, which has a CSS specificity of 0, so any selector you write will have higher specificity and easily override them. The styles target `[data-astro-image]` (applying `object-fit`/`object-position`) plus layout-specific rules such as `:where([data-astro-image='constrained']) { max-width: 100%; }`. You can also override `object-fit` and `object-position` per image with the `fit` and `position` props on `<Image />` or `<Picture />`.

Astro acts as the frontend presentation layer in a backend-service architecture. It consumes backend services (auth, databases, storage, monitoring) via integrations, handling UI rendering through its Islands Architecture — static HTML by default with selective hydration for interactive "islands." Astro's server islands (`server:defer`) can also run dynamic server-side code independently, but Astro itself does not manage backend infrastructure; it integrates with cloud backend services that provide that infrastructure.

Astro executes frontmatter JavaScript (between the `---` fences) on the server at render/build time. It runs before the template is rendered and is not available in the browser. Variables defined in frontmatter are used to generate the HTML output sent to the client.

The error "cannot read an implicit mapping pair; a colon is missed" indicates a missing colon (`:`) in a key-value pair within the Markdown frontmatter, such as `title "My Title"` instead of `title: "My Title"`.

The error "unexpected end of the stream within a double quoted scalar" indicates an unclosed or mismatched quote in a string value, like `description: "This is a description` (missing closing quote).

Both errors stem from invalid YAML syntax in the frontmatter block. Ensure all key-value pairs have proper colons and that all strings are properly quoted.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/markdown-frontmatter-parse-error/

Overriding the `nodes.image` node applies automatically to the native `![]()` syntax, but only carries `src` and `alt` — attributes like `width` or `height` cannot be expressed there. A custom `tags.image` tag is invoked explicitly (`{% image src="./astro-logo.png" alt="Astro Logo" width="100" caption="..." /%}`) and lets you declare extra `attributes` (e.g. `width`, `height`, `caption`, spread with `...nodes.image.attributes`) so your component can receive them — which is what makes Astro's `<Image />` usable for remote images that require `width` and `height`.

Importing an MDX file directly exposes both its `Content` component and its exported components as named imports — `import { Content, components } from '../content.mdx'` — so you can pass `<Content components={{...components, h1: Heading}} />`. A content collection entry is not imported directly; you fetch it with `getEntry()` and call `render(entry)` from `astro:content` to get `Content`, then supply any separately imported components through the `components` prop: `<Content components={{ h1: CustomHeading }} />`.

Setting recma plugins on `markdown.processor` still runs them for `.mdx` files, because MDX extends your Markdown configuration by default — this is the documented alternative to `mdx({ processor: unified({ recmaPlugins: [...] }) })`. The error "unexpected end of the stream within a double quoted scalar" occurs when YAML frontmatter contains an unclosed or malformed double-quoted string, often due to a missing closing quote.

Example problematic frontmatter:
```md
---
title: "This is a title
description: "A description"
---
```

Fix by ensuring all double-quoted strings are properly closed:
```md
---
title: "This is a title"
description: "A description"
---
```

Astro fails to parse the frontmatter section of a Markdown file when it encounters invalid syntax. Frontmatter must be valid YAML enclosed between `---` delimiters. Common causes include missing colons in key-value pairs, unmatched quotes, or incorrect indentation.

Example of problematic frontmatter:
```md
---
title: My Post
date: 2023-01-01
tags [invalid syntax]
---
```

Correct syntax should be:
```md
---
title: My Post
date: 2023-01-01
tags: [tag1, tag2]
---
```
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/markdown-frontmatter-parse-error/

This is the documented behavior for disabling sessions in Astro 7.2+.

This error occurs when YAML syntax in your Markdown frontmatter is invalid, such as missing colons, unquoted strings with special characters, or incorrect indentation.

To fix it, ensure all key-value pairs in frontmatter use a colon followed by a space (e.g., `title: "My Page"`), and that any strings containing special characters are properly quoted. Check for missing closing quotes on multiline strings or misplaced indentation in nested objects.

Example of valid frontmatter:
```md
---
title: "My Page"

tags: ["astro", "markdown"]
---

```

Loosening all fields in `src/content.config.*` to optional is the wrong fix when content entries must maintain a consistent structure for reliable rendering or data processing. This approach hides schema mismatches and can lead to runtime errors or missing data in components.

Instead, ensure each field matches the expected type and required status defined by the collection’s schema. For example, if `title` is required, it should be present in all entries. If a field like `pubDate` is optional, only omit it when explicitly allowed by the schema.

To resolve validation errors properly:

1. Review content entry files for missing or incorrectly typed fields.
2. Update the schema to reflect actual data requirements (e.g., make optional fields truly optional).
3. Use tools like globster.xyz to verify patterns and ensure correct file matching.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/invalid-content-entry-data-error/

Verify that the content entry file matches the schema defined in your `src/content.config.ts` file, including field names, types, and required fields. Ensure all required fields like `title` are present with correct data types (e.g., `z.string()`). Check for typos or incorrect formatting in the frontmatter or content file that might prevent proper parsing.

If using legacy collections (removed in Astro 6), ensure you're not mixing old syntax with new APIs. For current Astro versions, confirm your collection uses the Content Layer API and references `id` instead of `slug`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/invalid-content-entry-data-error/

Rendering a component with `` in an Astro template is the correct way to include it, while calling it directly as `Component()` inside an expression like `{items.map(Component)}` or `Component()` will cause an error. Astro components must be rendered using JSX-like syntax (``) within templates. When you use a component function directly (e.g., in a map), Astro throws an InvalidComponentArgs error because it cannot handle manual function calls of components. Example: ```astro ---import MyComponent from '../components/MyComponent.astro';---
    {items.map(item => )} {/* ✅ Correct */}
{/* ❌ Incorrect - will throw an error */} {items.map(Component)} ``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/invalid-component-args/

Astro components cannot be rendered manually via a function call like `{items.map(MyAstroComponent)}` because Astro requires explicit component syntax for rendering. The error occurs because `MyAstroComponent` is treated as a function rather than a component tag.

Instead, use the component syntax with JSX-like syntax: `{items.map(item => <MyAstroComponent {...item} />)`.

Example:
```astro
---import MyAstroComponent from '../components/MyAstroComponent.astro';---
{items.map(item => <MyAstroComponent {...item} />)}
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/invalid-component-args/

The `Aside.astro` component receives a `type` prop with the value `"tip"` (string). The tag's content (`content`) is passed to the component's default slot. Since the Markdoc config only defines a `type` attribute, the component does not receive `title` or `icon` props unless explicitly added to the tag.

You do not need the `@astrojs/netlify` adapter for a basic static site (`output: 'static'`). Install it only when you need Netlify-specific features: the Netlify Image CDN (for on-the-fly image optimization) or to translate Astro's `redirects` config into Netlify's `_redirects` file format.

The adapter writes `dist/_redirects` after `astro build`. Any redirects from `astro.config.mjs` are appended to the end of your `public/_redirects` file (if it exists), so manual redirects in `public/_redirects` take precedence.

The Netlify adapter automatically traces dependencies via static imports/requires, but does not detect files loaded dynamically through `fs` operations (e.g., `fs.readFile('./data/file.json')`). Data files accessed this way must be explicitly declared in `includeFiles` with glob patterns relative to the project root. If a new file isn't included, verify the glob pattern matches its path from root and that the file is actually read via `fs` at runtime.

Set `devFeatures.environmentVariables: true` in the Netlify adapter configuration. This injects environment variables from your linked Netlify site into local development. Requires `netlify link` to connect your local project to a Netlify site.

With `staticHeaders: false` (default), CSP is delivered via a `<meta http-equiv="content-security-policy">` tag in each page's HTML `<head>`. With `staticHeaders: true`, the adapter writes CSP as an actual HTTP response header in the platform's configuration (Netlify `_headers` or Vercel `vercel.json`), and the `<meta>` tag is omitted from static pages.

The adapter emulates Netlify Edge Functions by running them in a local sandbox during `astro dev` when `devFeatures.edgeFunctions: true` (default). Limitation: npm packages that perform filesystem access during initialization fail with "Reading or writing files with Edge Functions is not supported yet" because the edge function sandbox restricts filesystem operations. Disable with `devFeatures.edgeFunctions: false` and use `netlify dev` for local testing instead.

The error `IncorrectStrategyForI18n` occurs because your project’s `i18n.routing.strategy` is not set to `"manual"`, while your teammate's project likely has it set correctly or doesn't use i18n functions that require the manual strategy.

In Astro, certain internationalization helpers (like `getStaticPaths()` with localized routes) are only available when using `i18n.routing.strategy: "manual"`.

Check your `astro.config.mjs` for an `i18n` configuration block. If it's missing or has a different strategy like `"prefix-default"` or `"prefix-always"`, that explains why the functions fail in your project but not theirs.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/configuration-reference/#i18n

No, you should not switch `i18n.routing.strategy` to `"manual"`. When using the default i18n routing strategy (which is `prefixDefaultLocale: false` or `prefixDefaultLocale: true`), Astro automatically handles localized URL paths and routing. You can still call Astro's internationalization helper functions like `redirectToDefaultLocale()`, `notFound()`, and `redirectToFallback()` without needing to set `routing: "manual"`.

The `"manual"` strategy is only required if you want to implement custom routing logic instead of using Astro’s built-in i18n middleware. For standard use cases where you want automatic localization with access to helper functions, leave the default routing configuration in place.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/internationalization/#routing

When you set `i18n.routing.strategy` to `"manual"`, Astro disables its built-in i18n middleware, giving you full control over routing logic. You must handle locale detection, redirects, and fallbacks yourself using helper functions like `redirectToDefaultLocale()`, `notFound()`, or `redirectToFallback()`.

No other `routing` options (e.g., `prefixDefaultLocale`) can be used with `"manual"` strategy. You can still use the `middleware()` function manually to integrate Astro’s routing behavior alongside your custom logic, but you must manage all routing yourself otherwise.

Example config:
```js
i18n: {
  locales: ["es", "en", "fr"],
  defaultLocale: "en",
  routing: "manual"
}
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/internationalization/#routing

If you also specify `widths`, you’ll get an **IncompatibleDescriptorOptions** error because `densities` and `widths` cannot be used together—only one can define the `srcset` descriptor (`x` or `w`).

`extendMarkdownConfig: true` (default) makes MDX inherit the project's `markdown` config, letting you selectively override individual options like `syntaxHighlight` or `processor` in the MDX integration. `extendMarkdownConfig: false` completely disconnects MDX from the Markdown config — MDX uses its own defaults (e.g., default `satteri()` processor) and ignores all project-level Markdown settings unless you explicitly configure them in the MDX integration.
No. The optimizer automatically detects custom components exported via `export const components = { ... }` in the MDX file, so you don't need to manually configure `ignoreElementNames: ['h1']`.

Use `extendMarkdownConfig: false` when you want MDX to have a completely independent processing pipeline with no shared configuration — for example, to avoid inheriting a Unified-based processor when your Markdown uses Sätteri, or to prevent any project-level plugins, syntax highlighting, or remark/rehype settings from affecting `.mdx` files.

```astro
---
```

This Astro wrapper is then passed to `render` in the Markdoc config. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/markdoc/

Astro rejects an image that specifies both `densities` and `widths` because the two options are mutually exclusive when generating a `srcset` attribute. The `srcset` attribute cannot contain both `x` descriptors (used by `densities`) and `w` descriptors (used by `widths`). This is a limitation of the HTML standard, not Astro-specific.

Astro enforces this rule to prevent invalid markup and ensure correct behavior in responsive images. It does not silently pick one option because doing so could lead to unexpected rendering or performance issues due to conflicting image sizing instructions.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/incompatible-descriptor-options/

Astro automatically adds the header for built-in features (actions, server islands, view transitions, prefetch). For custom fetch calls, include the header manually: `'X-Netlify-Deploy-ID': import.meta.env.DEPLOY_ID`.

Use `widths` when you want to serve predefined pixel widths to the browser for responsive images in unpredictable container widths.

The `widths` prop generates a `srcset` with `w` descriptors (e.g., `100w`, `200w`) and requires a corresponding `sizes` attribute. This approach is ideal for your use case because it allows you to explicitly control the image sizes sent to the browser based on your layout needs.

You should avoid `densities` entirely when using predefined widths, as the two options are mutually exclusive and cannot be combined in a single `<Image>` component. Using both will result in an error: "Cannot set both densities and widths".

Example:
```astro
<Image
  src={myImage}
  widths={[300, 600, 900]}
  sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, (max-width: 1200px) 50vw, 33vw"
  alt="A description of my image."
/>
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-assets/#widths

You should NOT disable HTML streaming in Astro's Node adapter when you want components to render progressively and send HTML to the browser as soon as data is available, rather than waiting for all fetches to complete. Disabling streaming forces the server to wait for all data fetches to resolve before sending any HTML, blocking page rendering and increasing Time to First Byte (TTFB). Streaming allows parallel data fetching and incremental rendering — the `<head>`, static markup, and early components stream immediately while async components resolve in parallel.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/recipes/streaming-improve-page-performance/

`withState` preserves hidden form metadata (action name, serialized state) that enables the form to submit as a standard HTML POST request when JavaScript is disabled. With JS disabled, the browser submits the form to the action endpoint server-side; Astro executes the action handler, re-renders the page with updated state, and returns full HTML — progressive enhancement without client-side React.

For an image that conveys information only sighted users need, use `alt=""` to indicate it’s decorative and doesn’t contribute meaningfully to the page content. For a logo with visible text nearby, provide descriptive alt text that explains what the logo represents (e.g., "Company Name Logo") so screen reader users can understand its purpose.

Example:
```astro
<Image src={infoImage} alt="" />
<Image src={logoImage} alt="Company Name Logo" />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/images/#alt-text

Yes, Astro’s `<Image>` component will still throw the `ImageMissingAlt` error even if `alt=""` is passed, because the component requires an explicit `alt` prop to be present, regardless of its value.

For accessibility, setting `alt=""` on an image indicates that the image is decorative and should be ignored by screen readers. However, this must be explicitly provided as a string — omitting the prop entirely or passing `undefined` will trigger the error.

To avoid the error while maintaining proper accessibility semantics:

```astro
<Image src={post.coverImage} alt={post.coverAlt ?? ""} />
```

This ensures that even if `coverAlt` is missing, an empty string is passed, satisfying the component’s requirement and signaling to assistive technologies that the image is decorative.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/image-missing-alt/

It is correct to supply an empty `alt=""` on Astro’s `<Image />` component when the image is purely decorative and does not contribute meaningful content or information to the page. This tells screen readers to ignore the image, improving accessibility for users who rely on assistive technologies.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/image-missing-alt/

Pass `alt=""` to make an image purely decorative and skip it for screen readers. Omitting `alt` entirely or passing `alt={undefined}` fails because the Astro Image component requires the `alt` attribute to be present, even if empty.

Example:
```astro
<Image src={hero} alt="" />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/image-missing-alt/

The correct path for your image should be `./cover.png`, not `../images/cover.png`.

In Astro’s content collections, image paths in frontmatter are resolved relative to the `.md` file's location. Since your Markdown file is at `src/content/posts/weekly.md`, and the image is at `src/images/cover.png`, you need to go up one level from `weekly.md` to reach `src/`, then down into `images/`. That requires two `../` segments, making it `../../images/cover.png`.

However, because Astro resolves paths relative to the content collection entry (i.e., the `.md` file), and your image is in a sibling directory (`src/images/`), you should instead use `./cover.png`, which refers to the same location from within that context.

Example:
```ts
// src/content/posts/weekly.md
---
title: "Weekly Update"
cover: "./cover.png" // correct path for this file structure
---
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/images/#images-in-content-collections

Middleware mode does not serve static files — you must configure your HTTP framework (e.g., `express.static('dist/client/')`) to serve `dist/client/` before the SSR handler. Standalone mode serves static files automatically. This matters because in middleware mode, assets like `/_astro/...` will 404 unless your framework serves them explicitly.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/node/

Your Express middleware order is wrong. Static file serving (`express.static('dist/client/')`) must be registered **before** the Astro SSR handler. The handler only processes unmatched routes; if static middleware runs after, `/_astro/...` requests hit the handler and return 404.

```javascript
app.use(express.static('dist/client/')); // must be first
app.use(ssrHandler);
```
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/node/

The standalone server applies `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` to assets in `dist/client/_astro/`. This is appropriate because those assets are content-hashed (filename includes a hash), so they are immutable and safe to cache for a year.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/node/

`Could not find requested image 'IMAGE_PATH'. Does it exist?`

To avoid this issue, ensure all relative paths are updated or use absolute paths from your project's `public/` directory.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/image-not-found/

In **static mode**, dynamic routes require `getStaticPaths()` to define all possible paths at build time. For a CMS with tens of thousands of entries, this isn't feasible, so you must use **on-demand rendering** (`prerender = false`) instead.

With on-demand rendering, the route is served dynamically without needing `getStaticPaths()`. The page will respond to any matching URL pattern like `/resources/[resource]/[id]` at runtime. This approach works with adapters that support server-side rendering (SSR), such as Vercel or Netlify Functions.

In static mode:
- Use `getStaticPaths()` for known paths.
- Not suitable for large, dynamic datasets from a CMS.

In on-demand rendering (`prerender = false`):
- No need for `getStaticPaths()`.
- Pages are rendered at runtime when requested.
- Requires an adapter that supports SSR or serverless functions.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/routing/#dynamic-routes

`getActionState()` is designed to be used within the server-side action handler context and specifically with React components that integrate with Astro Actions via `@astrojs/react`. Using it outside of this context, such as in a standard Astro component or non-React environment, will result in an error because it relies on the internal state management provided by the React integration.

If you attempt to call `getActionState()` in a regular `.astro` file or a non-React component, it won't have access to the necessary context and will fail at runtime. It must be used inside an action handler where the request context is available through `AstroActionContext`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-actions/#getactionstate

When adding `@astrojs/solid-js` to an Astro project, the two required `tsconfig.json` compiler options are:

```json
{
  "jsx": "preserve",
  "jsxImportSource": "solid-js"
}
```

These settings ensure TypeScript properly handles SolidJS JSX syntax and knows to import JSX factories from `solid-js`.

No, the lazy component's HTML will not be included in the initial server-rendered page when using `client:only='solid'`.

Components with the `client:only` directive are rendered only on the client and are not processed during server-side rendering. As a result, any asynchronous operations or lazy-loaded components within them are also not executed or included in the initial HTML output.

Astro's automatic Suspense wrapping applies to server-rendered components (like those using `client:transparent` or `client:load`) but does not apply to `client:only` components. Therefore, even if a `client:only` Solid component uses lazy components, their HTML is not included in the initial SSR output.

Example:
```tsx
// This will NOT include the lazy component's HTML in SSR
<MySolidComponent client:only="solid" />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/#clientonly

To resolve this, install `react-compiler-runtime` to provide the necessary runtime support for older React versions:


When using `Astro.rewrite()` in an Astro 7 project with `output: 'server'`, avoid rewriting to routes marked as prerendered (e.g., using `export const prerender = true` or `prerender: true` in the page's frontmatter). Prerendered pages are compiled into static HTML files at build time and cannot be dynamically rewritten during runtime, which causes a ForbiddenRewrite error.

To prevent this issue:

1. **Do not mark pages as prerendered** if they will be used in `Astro.rewrite()` calls.
2. Ensure rewrite targets use dynamic rendering (on-demand routes) so that Astro can serve them at runtime.

Example:
```astro
---// src/pages/rewrite-target.astro
export const prerender = false; // Ensures it's not prerendered---
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/forbidden-rewrite/

Astro prevents `Astro.rewrite()` from targeting a route whose component is marked as prerendered when using the `"server"` output because prerendered routes are statically compiled into HTML files during the build process. These static files cannot be dynamically retrieved or rewritten at runtime, which is required for the rewrite operation.

To resolve this, ensure your route is not marked as prerendered (e.g., by removing `prerender: true` from its frontmatter) or use a server adapter that supports on-demand rendering to allow dynamic route handling. If using Starlight, you can customize route data instead of relying on rewrites.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/forbidden-rewrite/

Astro refuses the rewrite because `Astro.rewrite()` cannot map an on-demand route (like `/blog/[slug]`) to a static route (like `/about`) when using `"server"` output. Static routes are prerendered at build time into HTML files, which can't be dynamically served at runtime.

To fix this, make the target route (`/about`) also an on-demand route by using dynamic parameters or keeping it as a regular page that supports SSR. For example, rename `/about` to `/about/index.astro` or ensure it's not marked for prerendering in your config.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/forbidden-rewrite/

A `GenerateContentTypesError` during `astro sync` indicates that Astro failed to generate TypeScript types for your collections, likely due to an invalid schema definition or a mismatch in how entries are structured. Before rewriting your schemas, verify the following:

1. Ensure all collection entries match the defined Zod schema.
2. Confirm that no files violate the expected structure (e.g., missing required fields).
3. Check if any custom loaders like `generateId()` might be producing invalid IDs.

If those checks pass and you're confident in your schema, then consider reviewing or rewriting the schemas to ensure they align with actual entry data.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/generate-content-types-error/

The `GenerateContentTypesError` indicates that the `astro sync` command failed while trying to generate TypeScript types for content collections, likely due to a configuration or schema issue in your content files.

This error occurs during the type generation step of `astro sync`, which runs automatically when you execute `astro dev`, `astro build`, or `astro check`. It's not telling you exactly what went wrong with your content collection setup — that requires checking for specific errors like `InvalidContentEntryFrontmatterError` or `ContentCollectionMissingLoader`.

To resolve this, inspect the `<details>` section of the error message to identify which content collection failed and why. Common causes include invalid frontmatter in Markdown files, missing loaders, or mismatched schemas.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/generate-content-types-error/

Astro's `@astrojs/sitemap` integration cannot generate sitemap entries for dynamic routes in SSR mode because it relies on statically-generated routes during the build process. Pages rendered dynamically at request time in SSR mode are not known at build time, so they are excluded from the sitemap.

The recommended alternative is to use a custom `serialize()` function to manually add URLs for SSR-rendered pages, or ensure those pages are prerendered using on-demand rendering or static site generation (SSG) instead of server-side rendering (SSR). This allows the integration to discover and include them in the sitemap.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/sitemap/
