Import the endpoint's `GET` export and call it directly with the `Astro` global as its context, then read the JSON — no HTTP fetch involved: ```astro --- import { GET } from './api/hello.ts' let response = await GET(Astro) const data = await response.json() ---

{data.greeting} world!

``` This requires SSR (`output: 'server'`) or another on-demand rendering mode; in `static` mode the endpoint would need `export const prerender = false`. The endpoint file itself exports `GET: APIRoute` returning a `Response` (e.g. `new Response(JSON.stringify({ greeting: 'Hello' }))`).

The endpoint's `GET` handler is defined to receive a context object (similar to `APIContext`) containing properties like `request` and `params`. The `Astro` global provides that request context, so you pass it as the argument to give the handler access to the incoming request data. Without it, the handler would lack the context it expects.

Calling `GET(Astro)` directly executes the handler within the same server-side rendering context, without requiring an additional fetch request. This avoids the network overhead of an HTTP round-trip to the running server. Both approaches execute on the server during SSR, but the direct call skips serialization over the network.

When the request must originate from the browser rather than the server. For example, client-side file uploads require the browser to fetch an auth token endpoint directly (e.g., `fetch('/api/upload-auth')`) so the returned credentials can be passed to a client-side upload library. The server cannot make that call on behalf of the browser.

The `logger.config` must be a plain serializable object (`Record<string, unknown>`). Ensure all values are JSON-serializable primitives (strings, numbers, booleans) or plain objects/arrays — avoid functions, class instances, or other non-serializable types. The `entrypoint` must be a string or URL pointing to a JavaScript file.

The error means `paginate()`'s page-number param was not found in your filepath, so the route file itself must contain a matching dynamic segment: keep the folder named exactly `[page]`, as in `src/pages/blog/page/[page]/index.astro`. If the bracketed name in the path doesn't match the `PARAM_NAME` Astro looks for, `PageNumberParamNotFound` is thrown. Once the segment is present, each generated route receives the `page` prop — `page.data`, `page.currentPage`, `page.lastPage`, `page.url.prev`, `page.url.next` — for building navigation.

`public/robots.txt` tells search bots how to crawl and index your site (e.g. `User-agent: *` with `Allow: /`), and Astro never processes anything in `public/`: those files are served at `/` during dev and copied to the build directory as-is, without transform or bundling (`publicDir` defaults to `"./public"`). That makes `public/` ideal for special files such as `robots.txt` and `manifest.webmanifest`, plus images and fonts needing no processing — CSS and JavaScript you write yourself belong in `src/`, since `public/` files ship unbundled.

A hardcoded URL like `/logo.png` gets no build-time image processing: images in `public/` are never optimized, and responsive images are not supported for them, so the raw file is used as-is. Importing the asset in frontmatter instead — `import myImage from '../assets/my_image.png'` rendered with `<Image src={myImage} alt="A description of my image." layout="constrained" width={800} height={600} />` from `astro:assets` — makes Astro process it, emitting a hashed optimized output such as `/_astro/my_image.hash3.webp` and, with `layout` set, generating `srcset`/`sizes`. On prerendered pages those variants are created during the build (increasing build time); with on-demand rendering they're generated when a page is visited.

Because files in `public/` are copied directly to the output directory and are not processed by Rollup, so `assetFileNames` (or any `rollupOptions.output` naming pattern) does not apply to them. `entryFileNames` names JavaScript entry files — scripts directly associated with your pages or layouts (e.g. `js/[name]-[hash].js`). `chunkFileNames` names JavaScript code-split chunks — dynamically imported components or shared modules (e.g. `js/chunks/[name]-[hash].js`). Use `entryFileNames` to control top-level page/script outputs, and `chunkFileNames` to organize split/shared code, often under a separate `chunks/` directory. Both are set under `vite.environments.client.build.rollupOptions.output` (the Astro 6+ location; previously `vite.build.rollupOptions.output` in Astro 5.x) and support `[name]` and `[hash]` placeholders.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/recipes/customizing-output-filenames/

{inputErrors.email &&

Astro throws `LocalsNotAnObject` because `context.locals` must remain an object; assigning a non-object value (e.g. `context.locals = 1541`) overwrites it with something Astro rejects. Since Astro 5.0, replacing the whole object is also forbidden and throws `LocalsReassigned`, as that would wipe information stored by integrations or earlier middleware.

`context.locals` is the supported request-scoped store: it is forwarded through the request handling process and exposed on `APIContext` and `AstroGlobal`, so middleware-written values are readable in `.astro` files (`Astro.locals`) and API routes, and shared between middlewares. A regular variable in the middleware file isn't exposed through those APIs. `locals` lives and dies within a single route — a new one is created per request — so information needing persistence across requests must be stored elsewhere; it also must stay an object and cannot be overridden at runtime.

Passing the function directly would hand `<Image>` a function instead of an image, so the recipe explicitly requires you to "invoke the glob function": `<Image src={images[imagePath]()} alt={altText} />`.

Replace the single `*` with `/**/*`: `/src/assets/**/*.{jpeg,jpg,png,gif}`. The `/**` segment looks through all subdirectories (as in `./pages/**/*.{md,mdx}`), while `/*` still matches any filename and the `.{jpeg,jpg,png,gif}` brace group keeps the same extension list — so `src/assets/team/avatar-1.jpg` is included.

`entrypointResolution: "explicit"` is the default value that mimics Astro 5.x adapter API behavior (using `createExports()` and `start()`). It is deprecated and will be removed in a future major version in favor of `entrypointResolution: "auto"`.

To migrate:
1. Set `entrypointResolution: "auto"` in `setAdapter()` and remove `exports` and `args`.
2. Replace `createExports()` in your server entrypoint with `createApp()` from `astro/app/entrypoint`.
3. If you had a `start()` function, call its code directly in the entrypoint.
4. If you relied on `args`, create a virtual module to pass build-time configuration and import from it instead.

`Astro.redirect()` returns a `Response` that navigates the browser to a new URL, optionally with a custom status code (defaults to `302`). For on-demand rendered routes, custom status codes are supported; for statically-generated routes, it produces a client-side `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` redirect without status code support.

`Astro.rewrite()` serves a different route's content at the current URL without a client-side navigation. However, it cannot rewrite an on-demand route to a static (prerendered) route when using `output: 'server'`, as the static component is compiled to an HTML file at build time and cannot be retrieved at runtime.

They are the same method — `redirect()` returns a `Response`, available on the `Astro` global in pages and on the context object in endpoints and middleware — but usage differs by rendering context. In a page component, the page itself (not a child component) must `return Astro.redirect(...)`, since HTML streaming in on-demand rendering requires redirects at page level. In an API route, you return `redirect("/login", 302)` directly as your handler's response. Behavior depends on rendering: statically-generated routes produce a client-side `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` redirect with no status code support, while on-demand routes support custom status codes (default `302`).

Three scripts cover the standard local workflow:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "astro dev",
    "build": "astro build",
    "preview": "astro preview"
  }
}
```

- `dev` runs `astro dev`, the development server with a live preview that updates as you edit.
- `build` runs `astro build`, producing a deploy-ready site in `dist/` (default) and surfacing build errors; with TypeScript set to `strict` or `strictest`, it also checks the project for type errors.
- `preview` runs `astro preview`, serving the built site locally.

The `create astro` wizard adds these automatically; add them yourself during manual setup, plus any extra commands you use often.

Astro stopped the build and reported the underlying error instead of writing `dist/` — commonly an *unknown filesystem error* (reading/writing files, e.g. missing permissions or a nonexistent file), an *unknown Markdown error* (usually a syntax error, with details in the message), or an *unknown Vite error* while rendering your project. Catching it here matters because the build alerts you to errors **before you deploy to production**, and with TypeScript configured to `strict` or `strictest` the `build` script also checks your project for type errors — so a broken build never reaches your host.

- **Live edits:** `npm run dev` (`astro dev`) — the dev server shows a live preview that updates as you edit files in `src/`.
- **Deploy-ready output:** `npm run build` (`astro build`) — writes the production site to `dist/` by default, with built assets like JS/CSS placed in an `_astro/` directory under hashed filenames.
- **Most recent build only:** `npm run preview` (`astro preview`) — serves the built site exactly as it existed when `build` last ran; changes made after building are not reflected until you rebuild.

After a rebuild, commit and push so your host can deploy the updated output.

`Astro.logger` messages carry one of three levels — `error`, `warn`, `info` (highest to lowest) — and only messages at or above the configured logger `level` (default `info`) are printed, so `logger: logHandlers.json({ level: "warn" })` suppresses `info`. The destination determines output: `logHandlers.console()` maps `error` to `console.error()`, `warn` to `console.warn()`, `info` to `console.info()`; the default `logHandlers.node()` writes `error` to `stderr` and the rest to `stdout`; `logHandlers.json()` prints `{ message, label, level, time }`. A custom logger takes over all logs, including yours, so its `write()` should check `matchesLevel(message.level, level)` from `astro/logger`.

Awaiting fetches in a page's frontmatter blocks the whole response: Astro waits for all `fetch` calls to resolve before sending any HTML. Moving the fetches into child components lets Astro's HTML streaming work for you — the page shell (`<head>`, `<body>`, headings) renders immediately, then the child fetches run in parallel and their HTML streams to the browser as each resolves. Including promises directly in the template is a middle ground: earlier markup renders right away and only the markup after the promise blocks until it settles.

Astro scoped styles only match elements carrying the parent's `data-astro-cid-*` scope attribute, and HTML attributes like `class` don't automatically pass through to child components — so the child's `<button class="button">` sits outside the parent's scope and `.button { color: red; }` never matches it. Two fixes:

1. Accept the class in the child, rename it (it's a reserved word), and spread the rest of the props so the scope attribute is forwarded:

```astro
---
const { class: className, ...rest } = Astro.props;
---

Use the path without the trailing slash (`'/product1'`) as the redirect key instead. Redirects must map a route to the same kind of route (static to static, dynamic to dynamic with matching parameters).

Setting `i18n.routing: "manual"` disables Astro's built-in i18n middleware so you can implement your own custom logic; no other `routing` options (e.g. `prefixDefaultLocale`) may be combined with it. You are responsible for providing your own middleware file — Astro throws `MissingMiddlewareForInternationalization` if none exists. You can write your own routing logic from scratch, or execute Astro's i18n middleware manually via the `middleware()` function from `astro:i18n` (combined with your own middleware using `sequence()`). Helper functions are available for your middleware: `redirectToDefaultLocale()`, `notFound()`, and `redirectToFallback()`.

Configure `session.ttl` in your `astro.config.mjs`. It is expressed in **seconds**; for a one-hour default, set `ttl: 3600`. The default is `Infinity` (values persist until deleted or the session is destroyed). Passing a `ttl` option to `session.set()` overrides the global default for that individual entry. Note that setting `ttl` does not automatically delete the value from storage — it is only deleted when accessed after the expiry period, at which point the value is `undefined`.

Static sites without an adapter use client-side `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` redirects because there's no server to emit HTTP status codes. To get real 301/308 responses, enable SSR (`output: 'server'`) or add a static adapter (e.g., `@astrojs/netlify`, `@astrojs/vercel`) with `output: 'static'`. Adapters provide the server infrastructure needed to serve proper HTTP redirects.

Run `astro telemetry enable` to turn telemetry back on. The setting is stored per CLI user, not per project: `astro telemetry` sets telemetry configuration for the current CLI user, so the enabled/disabled state applies across all of your projects on that machine. The anonymous data it reports gives the Astro team insight into which Astro features are most used.

`astro telemetry disable` stops Astro from sending telemetry at all (re-enable with `astro telemetry enable`, or set `ASTRO_TELEMETRY_DISABLED` in CI environments). `astro telemetry reset` only resets the telemetry data that has already been collected — it does not affect whether new data is sent. Both commands configure telemetry for the current CLI user.

Use `astro check --noSync`, which specifies that `astro sync` should not run before checking the project. It is safe when generated types are already current for your sources — e.g., your CI's preceding `astro sync` step has just run and nothing changed afterward. Keep in mind that `sync` generates `.astro/types.d.ts` plus the `astro:content`, `astro:env`, and `astro:actions` modules; if those types are missing or stale, `astro check` will report diagnostics against outdated type definitions, so re-run `astro sync` whenever type-relevant files change.

Server renderers must be added before client renderers because the rendering pipeline executes in two phases: first the **entire container renders statically on the server** (producing HTML), then **client hydration runs** for any interactive islands. Adding server renderers first ensures all components are available for the initial server render pass before client entrypoints are registered for subsequent hydration.

When a live loader's `loadEntry()` returns a `LiveDataEntry` with the optional `rendered` property set to `{ html: string }`, that HTML is stored with the entry, which enables both `render()` and `<Content />` for rendering the body in a page:

```astro
---
import { getLiveEntry, render } from 'astro:content';
const entry = await getLiveEntry('posts', 'welcome');
const { Content } = await render(entry);
---
<Content />
```

If `rendered` is omitted, `<Content />` renders nothing. Since `rendered` was added in `astro@6.0.0`, this applies to live loaders in Astro 6+.

`store.set()` returns `false` because the `digest` you supply matches the digest of the existing entry with the same ID: the entry only updates when the digest differs from the stored one, so a fresh `DataEntry` with an unchanged (or identical) digest is skipped. Digest comparison is a plain string comparison — the entry's `digest` string is compared against the stored entry's `digest`, and only a mismatch triggers the update; the format is loader-defined but must change when the data changes. Use `generateDigest(data)` to compute it:

```ts
const digest = generateDigest(data);
store.set({ id, data, digest });
```

If data changed but `set()` still returns `false`, the digest is not actually reflecting that change.

`rendered.metadata.headings` is a `MarkdownHeading[]` describing each heading in the rendered Markdown: each entry has a `depth` from the heading level (`h1`–`h6`), a `slug`, and its `text` content. The `slug` is generated with [`github-slugger`](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger). This metadata is `undefined` when the content has not been rendered as HTML.

If a `DataEntry` lacks the `rendered` property, the `<Content />` component will render nothing. The `<Content />` component is only available when `rendered` is provided. To render the raw `body` field instead, output it directly in your template (e.g., `{entry.body}`) or use a custom component that renders the raw string.

It unblocks the build, but it's masking the real problem rather than fixing it. With `'ignore'`, the build silently uses the highest-priority route, so one of your two routes never emits its page — a static path can only be generated by one route, and you'll never hear about the duplicate again. The durable fix is resolving the conflict itself (rename or remove one of the colliding routes). If you must ship immediately, switch to `'warn'` (the default): it also unblocks the build but still logs each conflict so you can fix them before the next release. `'ignore'` gives you no signal at all.

2. **`astro:server:setup`** — receive a `toolbar` object with `send()`, `on()`, `onAppInitialized()`, `onAppToggled()` to push data to the client and listen for messages.

The app icon shows an "error"-level notification highlight: a dark pink circle. With no properties passed, `toggleNotification({})` assumes `state: true`, so the icon is highlighted, and `level: 'error'`, which determines the color and shape of the highlight (dark pink circle for error, gold triangle for warning, blue square for info).

On the client, use the `server` object passed as the third argument to `init()`: call `server.send('my-app:my-message', payload)` to send a message, and register `server.on('server-message', (data) => {...})` to receive the response. Prefix client event names with your app ID to avoid conflicts. On the server, use the `astro:server:setup` integration hook's `toolbar` object: `toolbar.on('my-app:my-message', callback)` handles incoming messages, and `toolbar.send('server-message', payload)` sends the response back. `beforeTogglingOff()` is an optional hook that runs when the user clicks the app icon to toggle the app off, letting you perform cleanup or ask for confirmation first. It receives the app's `canvas` ShadowRoot and may return a boolean or a `Promise<boolean>`. A falsy return value cancels the action, so the toggling off is cancelled and the app stays enabled; a truthy value lets the toggle proceed. Example: return `window.confirm("Really exit?")` so the user can decline.

`Loader.name` is a unique string identifier for your build-time loader (added in `astro@5.0.0`). Astro uses it in logs and for conditional loading — specifically the `refreshContent` option of integrations, which can target loaders by name to decide which collections to reload. It is one of the two required properties of a `Loader` object, alongside `load()`.

Astro provides two built-in loaders for local content: `glob()` and `file()`. The `glob()` loader fetches entries from directories of Markdown, MDX, Markdoc, JSON, YAML, or TOML files using a glob pattern and base path. The `file()` loader loads a single file. Both are object loaders provided out-of-the-box for local content. Custom object loaders require implementing a `Loader` object with a `load()` method, `name`, and optional `schema`/`createSchema()` for remote data sources (CMS, APIs, databases), and must manually interact with the data store via `store.set()` and `store.clear()`.

You can use the async function directly as a loader. For simple data fetching, define the loader as an async function that returns an array of entries with a unique `id` field, or an object with IDs as keys. At build time, Astro automatically clears the data store and reloads all entries. This shorthand requires no `load()` method, `store.set()`, or `Loader` object — just return the data. Example: `loader: async () => { const res = await fetch(url); return res.json().map(item => ({ id: item.id, ...item })); }`.

The `rootMargin` option in `client:visible` expands the IntersectionObserver's trigger area. When set (e.g., `rootMargin: "200px"`), the component hydrates when a 200px margin *around* the component enters the viewport, not when the component itself becomes visible. This gives the component more time to download and hydrate before the user scrolls to it, reducing layout shift (CLS) on slow connections. Increase the value (e.g., `"300px"` or `"500px"`) to start hydration even earlier.

MiddlewareNotAResponse means your middleware returned a non-Response value. Your `onRequest` function must return a Response object — either directly (`new Response(...)`) or by calling `next()` and returning its result.

Astro forbids `rewrite()` after reading the request body because the body stream is consumed. The correct pattern is to clone the request first: `const data = await Astro.request.clone().json();` then call `Astro.rewrite('/target')`.

Astro requires an adapter for server islands because they use the same on-demand rendering infrastructure as SSR. Server islands are split into separate routes that are fetched at runtime, which requires a server adapter to handle the deferred rendering. Without an adapter installed, you'll get the error: "Cannot use server islands without an adapter. Please install and configure the appropriate server adapter for your final deployment."

Add an `X-Robots-Tag` header in a server-rendered page or endpoint by setting the header on the response. In an Astro page component with `output: "server"`, use `Astro.response.headers.set()`:

```astro
---
export const prerender = false;
Astro.response.headers.set("X-Robots-Tag", "noindex, nofollow");
---
<html>...</html>
```

For non-HTML resources (PDFs, images), the HTTP header is the only way to control indexing.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/seo/meta-robots/

`Astro.callAction()` is required when calling actions from server-rendered pages or endpoints. Directly calling an action function (e.g., `actions.logout()`) from server code throws `ActionCalledFromServerError`. `callAction()` wraps the invocation to properly handle the action's lifecycle, returning `{ data, error }` as a promise. Use it in `.astro` components or server endpoints via `context.callAction()`.

```astro
---
import { actions } from 'astro:actions';
const { data, error } = await Astro.callAction(actions.logout, { userId: '123' });
---
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/action-called-from-server-error/

Astro 6.0 removed the experimental `headingIdCompat` flag by making its behavior the default: heading IDs ending in special characters now keep their trailing hyphens instead of having them stripped, matching `github-slugger` (and thus GitHub/npm) slugs. In Astro 5.x a default processing step stripped those trailing hyphens, which could make IDs diverge across platforms; expect IDs for headings like `## Some heading!` to now end in `-` (e.g. `some-heading--` style slugs retaining the hyphen) rather than being trimmed. Since the compat behavior is now always on, anchors generated in 5.x that relied on stripped hyphens may need updating, and `getHeadings()` will reflect the github-slugger values.

`MiddlewareNoDataOrNextCalled` is thrown when your middleware's `onRequest` handler completes without returning anything and without calling `next()`—it must return a `Response` directly or return the `Response` from `next()`. `EndpointDidNotReturnAResponse` is thrown when an endpoint (e.g. a `GET` export) returns nothing or returns something that is not a `Response` object; it must return a `Response` or a `Promise<Response>`.

In short: the first is a middleware that neither responds nor delegates; the second is an endpoint that doesn't produce a `Response`. (A related `MiddlewareNotAResponse` is thrown in dev when middleware returns a non-`Response` value such as a string.)

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/error-reference/

`define:vars` is the exception to the rule that any extra attribute on `<style>` implies `is:inline` — so your styles are still processed normally: bundled, optimized, and scoped to the component, rather than left as-is in the final HTML. The frontmatter values are serialized with `JSON.stringify()` and injected as CSS custom properties, which you consume with `var(--name)`:

```astro
<style define:vars={{ textColor: foregroundColor, backgroundColor }}>
  h1 { background-color: var(--backgroundColor); color: var(--textColor); }
</style>
```

(The `<script>` tag behaves differently: `define:vars` there does imply `is:inline`, so scripts are not bundled.)

Import the stylesheet from the component's frontmatter instead, and Astro will bundle and optimize it:

```astro

---
```

Put the directive on the tag itself:

```astro

```

Use server actions when you want the submission handled on the server with validation and zero-JS capability; use plain client-side functions only when no server work is needed. With an action, a `<form method="POST" action={actions.logout}>` submits without client JavaScript, and the server parses and validates the data via the action's `input` schema:

```astro
---
import { actions } from 'astro:actions';
---
<form method="POST" action={actions.logout}>
  <button>Log out</button>
</form>
```

The page calling the action via form `action` must be on-demand rendered (prerendering disabled). Client-side functions are still useful for in-browser behavior such as calling `actions.newsletter(formData)` then `navigate('/confirmation')` — but the actual mutation should live in the action.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/

Handlers must return serializable data types: objects, arrays, strings, and numbers; they cannot return a `Response`. (This differs from Astro pages, where only a `Response` may be returned.) Convert the value to plain data before returning, or use `Astro.redirect()` on the calling page instead of returning a redirect `Response` from the handler.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/actions-returned-invalid-data-error/

`ActionsCantBeLoaded` indicates that an unknown error was thrown while loading the Astro actions file. It is thrown exclusively in development mode when the actions file cannot be loaded at all — meaning the module fails to parse or execute during import, before any individual action is invoked.

`ActionsCantBeLoaded` occurs at module load time in development, when the actions file itself fails to load — no request has been processed yet. A runtime error inside an action handler occurs later, during request execution, when the handler is actually invoked. Handler errors (including thrown `ActionError` instances) are caught and returned as the `error` property of the `{ data, error }` result, whereas `ActionsCantBeLoaded` prevents the actions module from loading entirely.

`import.meta.glob()` is not a drop-in when the pattern cannot be a static string literal — it only supports static glob patterns, never dynamic variables or string interpolation, so a loader that builds its pattern at runtime must glob a wider set and filter instead. It is also unsuitable for content that isn't local files: remote/CMS data, or builds needing queryable, cacheable access to thousands of entries at scale — the cases `getCollection()` and content loaders are designed for.

Because `Astro.response.headers` is a `readonly Headers` instance on the `ResponseInit` object: individual headers can be added to and removed from it, but it must not be replaced with another instance of `Headers` altogether — reassignment throws `AstroResponseHeadersReassigned`. Set the header by mutating the existing instance instead:

```astro
---
Astro.response.headers.set('X-Custom', 'value');
---
```

Assigning a new `Headers` object to `Astro.response.headers` throws `AstroResponseHeadersReassigned`, because Astro requires the original `Headers` instance on its `ResponseInit` object to remain in place. Astro prevents replacing the entire `Headers` instance on `Astro.response.headers` because the `response` object is typed as `ResponseInit & { readonly headers: Headers }`, making `headers` readonly. The `readonly` modifier allows mutation of the existing `Headers` instance (via `append()`, `set()`, `delete()`) but blocks reassignment to a new `Headers` object. This design ensures Astro's internal response handling maintains a stable reference to the headers object while still permitting header modifications.

Fix the path, or use `import type { ... }` for type-only imports.

Use a type-only import with the `import type` syntax, which erases the import at compile time so nothing is resolved at runtime:

```astro
---
import type { Props as CardProps } from "./types";
---
```

For contrast, a value import such as `import { getUser } from './user'` is emitted into the SSR module graph and will fail if the path is wrong or the export doesn't exist at runtime.

Correct the import path when the file genuinely cannot be resolved — the target file doesn't exist or the path has a typo. Mark it as a type import (`import type { ... }`) when the path resolves fine but the imported symbol is TypeScript-only, so the runtime import has no corresponding JavaScript export to load. Also remember not to use `.ts`/`.tsx` extensions in import specifiers; omit the extension or use `.js`/`.jsx`.

The fundamental difference lies in when and how HTML is generated: `<Avatar server:defer>` defers **server-side rendering** until the client requests it, using a server island; `<ReactComponent client:visible />` renders **static HTML on the server**, then sends JavaScript to hydrate the component when visible.

</BaseLayout>
```

Astro 7's server-first rendering model differs from traditional server-side frameworks by allowing developers to write components in standard HTML, JavaScript, or TypeScript without requiring a runtime environment on the server. Instead of writing full server-side code like PHP or Laravel, developers use Astro’s component syntax with directives such as `server:defer` for server islands.

This approach enables static generation and on-demand rendering while maintaining developer familiarity with web technologies. The key advantage is that it provides a more streamlined development experience by reducing the complexity of managing server-side logic and allowing faster build-time optimizations, all while preserving performance benefits like partial hydration and dynamic content loading.

Astro's model also supports hybrid deployments where parts of a page are rendered statically or on-demand, offering flexibility similar to modern frameworks but with simpler tooling and fewer runtime dependencies. This makes it easier for developers who want fast sites without sacrificing the ease of writing web components in familiar languages like JavaScript or TypeScript.

Astro offers two distinct approaches for adding client-side interactivity to static pages: **UI framework components with `client:` directives** and **Astro `<script>` tags within components**.

1. **UI Framework Components (`client:` directive)**  
   Use a UI framework component (e.g., React, Vue) with a `client:` directive like `client:visible` or `client:idle`. This hydrates only that specific component on the client side, sending minimal JavaScript for just that component’s interactivity. The rest of the page remains static HTML.

2. **Astro `<script>` Tags**  
   Add inline `<script is:inline>` to an Astro component. This executes JavaScript directly in the browser and can manipulate DOM elements or manage state within that component's scope, but does not require a framework. It’s ideal for simple interactions like theme toggling.

These approaches differ from a full client-side SPA because they allow selective hydration of components rather than hydrating entire pages or apps, reducing JavaScript payload size and improving performance by defaulting to static rendering.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-components/

A realistic project where a mostly content-driven Astro site needs dynamic pages is a documentation or knowledge base platform with user-specific content, such as personalized dashboards or versioned API references.

In this scenario, static pages handle general content like "Getting Started" guides and "API Overview", while dynamic routes manage user-specific views (e.g., `/user/[id]/dashboard`) or versioned docs (`/docs/[version]/api-reference`). Astro's server-first rendering allows these dynamic pages to be rendered on the server for each request, enabling real-time data fetching and authentication checks. Static pages are pre-rendered at build time, while dynamic routes use `getStaticPaths()` with props to generate specific content based on parameters like user ID or version.

This hybrid approach lets developers optimize performance by prerendering most content statically while still supporting personalized or frequently updated sections dynamically through server-side rendering (SSR) or edge functions. The same project can include both static and dynamic pages, leveraging Astro's flexibility in routing and data handling without needing separate frameworks or complex setups.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/routing/

In Astro, files are processed at build time based on their extension and location.

- **Astro components** (`*.astro`) are rendered to static HTML and never sent to the browser as written.
- **JavaScript/TypeScript files** (`*.js`, `*.ts`) are bundled and sent to the browser if imported into a `<script>` tag or used in client-side code.
- **CSS files** (`*.css`) are sent to the browser, optimized, and bundled.

Files like `src/components/Menu.astro` are rendered to static HTML at build time, while `src/scripts/menu.js` is sent to the browser when imported into a `<script>` tag.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/tutorial/3-components/4/

In Astro, "reserved" means certain directory names have special meaning or functionality built into the framework, while others are conventional but not enforced.

`src/pages/` is reserved because Astro automatically treats files inside it as pages for routing — this behavior is part of how Astro builds your site. Other directories like `src/components/`, `src/layouts/`, and even `src/assets/` are conventions used by developers to organize code, but they're not required or enforced by Astro itself.

If you delete `src/components/` or `src/layouts/`, any files that import from those paths will fail because the imports no longer resolve — this isn't due to Astro reserving these folders, but rather how your project's structure and imports are set up. You can rename or restructure directories as long as all references match.

Astro only reserves specific folder names for its own functionality: `src/pages/`, `src/middleware.ts/js`, and now `src/fetch.ts/js` (since v7). Everything else is flexible, though following conventions helps with maintainability.

`astro preview` serves the static output from `dist/` to simulate a production build, while `astro dev` offers live reloading during development. This design reflects their distinct roles: `astro dev` is for iterative coding with instant feedback, and `astro preview` ensures accurate pre-deployment validation of the final built output.

The key architectural difference lies in how each command handles updates:
- `astro dev` runs a development server that watches files and injects HMR (Hot Module Replacement) scripts to update the browser without full reloads.
- `astro preview` starts a static file server pointing at the built assets, which are generated once by `astro build`. It does not watch for changes or enable live updates.

This distinction supports the workflow where `astro dev` enables rapid iteration and debugging during development, while `astro preview` mimics production behavior to catch any discrepancies before deployment. The lack of live reloading in `preview` ensures that developers can verify how their site behaves after all optimizations and transformations are applied — such as minification or prerendering.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/cli-reference/#astro-preview

Running `npm run preview` after a build lets you locally simulate how your site will behave once deployed, checking the final output in a production-like environment. It shows how the built files (`dist/`) appear when served statically, helping catch issues before deployment.

Deploying to the web (e.g., Netlify) makes your site live and accessible online, verifying that your hosting provider correctly serves the built assets and handles routing, SSL, etc. The preview is for local validation; deployment confirms everything works in a real production environment.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/develop-and-build/

Additionally, dev mode uses Vite's development server which may behave differently than your final deployment environment.

To test caching locally, build and preview your site using `astro build && astro preview`. This ensures that the production-like behavior of your routes is tested before deploying.

For deployment-specific concerns like Deno Deploy, ensure you're testing with a full build step (`npm run build`) followed by running the built output in a similar environment to what will be used in production. For example:

```bash
deno run -A ./dist/server/entry.mjs
```

Use **editor extensions** (e.g., VS Code) to enhance your coding workflow by providing syntax highlighting, auto-completion for Astro components, quick navigation, and integration with Astro’s CLI commands from within the editor. These are useful during authoring and editing phases.

Choose the dev toolbar when you need runtime visibility into how your app behaves; choose editor extensions when working on code or setting up new projects.

First, stop the development server with `Ctrl` + `C`. Then run `npm run build`, `pnpm build`, or `yarn run build` depending on your package manager. Finally, run `npm run preview`, `pnpm preview`, or `yarn run preview` to start a local server that serves the built files from the `dist/` directory.

The `preview` command must come after `build` because it serves the static output generated by `astro build`. The `build` command compiles your site into deployable assets in the `dist/` folder, and `preview` serves those specific files locally to simulate how your site will appear when deployed. Running `preview` before `build` would result in an empty or missing server since no built output exists yet.

Example:
```bash
# After stopping dev server
npm run build
npm run preview
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/develop-and-build/

Astro's build process generates a deploy-ready static version of your site in the `dist/` directory to ensure that all assets, pages, and content are fully compiled and optimized before being deployed. This separation allows for clean, production-ready output that can be served by any static hosting provider.

The `build` command creates this static output in `dist/`, including prerendered HTML files, bundled JavaScript, and copied assets. The `preview` command then serves this built content locally from the same directory, enabling you to test how your site will behave once deployed without needing a live development server or additional setup.

This workflow ensures consistency between local testing and production deployment by isolating the build output from the dev environment.

The likely reason Stylelint isn't reporting issues in `<style>` blocks within `.astro` files is that `stylelint-config-html` is designed for standalone HTML files and doesn't integrate with Astro's component parsing or AST traversal logic. Astro components require specific processors or plugins to analyze embedded styles, which this configuration package does not provide.

The `stylelint-config-html` package enables linting of CSS within `<style>` tags in standard HTML documents by applying Stylelint rules to HTML-style syntax. However, it lacks support for Astro's unique structure where styles are embedded inside component frontmatter or script blocks and must be processed through Astro’s own pipeline.

To lint embedded styles in `.astro` files, you should configure a plugin like `stylelint-processor-html` that understands how to parse and analyze CSS within Astro components. Alternatively, consider using Astro's built-in styling features with tools such as PostCSS or Tailwind CSS for better integration and linting support.

Example:
```astro
<form method="POST" action={actions.upload} enctype="multipart/form-data">

  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>
```

Using `getActionContext()` in middleware to validate sessions before actions run allows centralized, reusable logic across multiple actions, improving maintainability and enforcing security at the request level. It avoids duplicating session checks inside each action handler.

In contrast, performing authorization checks directly within an action handler using `context.locals.user` keeps validation logic co-located with the action but can lead to code duplication if many actions require similar checks.

A key limitation of the middleware approach is that it does not provide access to the actual action result (e.g., return value from the action) until after the action has run. This makes it difficult to perform conditional logic based on results, such as logging or redirecting depending on whether an action succeeded or failed.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-actions/

You should use `.orThrow()` when you want to skip explicit error handling and let errors propagate as thrown exceptions, such as during prototyping or when using a library that handles errors for you. It is appropriate when you're confident the action will succeed or when error handling is managed elsewhere.

If successful, `.orThrow()` returns the `data` property directly, with the type matching the return type of the action's `handler`.

Example:
```ts
const result = await actions.likePost.orThrow({ postId: '123' });
// result is of type number (from handler)
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/

In `src/pages/products.astro`, when `Astro.url.searchParams.get('search')` returns `null`, the condition `if (searchQuery)` evaluates to false because `null` is falsy in JavaScript.

As a result, the code inside the `if` block — including the call to `Astro.callAction(actions.findProduct, { query: searchQuery })` — is never executed. This behavior ensures that actions are only invoked when there's an actual search query present.

This pattern prevents unnecessary or invalid action calls when no search term is provided.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/

The recommended pattern is to use the `.orThrow()` property on your action call. This throws errors instead of returning them, allowing direct access to the `data` property without needing to check for errors or undefined values.

Example:
```ts
const updatedLikes = await actions.likePost.orThrow({ postId: 'example' });
```

This approach skips error handling and directly returns the typed `data` from the action's handler. It’s useful during prototyping or when using libraries that handle errors automatically. For production code, explicitly checking for errors is still preferred to ensure robust error management.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/#handling-returned-data

The choice between `actions.logout()` and `Astro.callAction(actions.findProduct, {...})` depends on the context: server-rendered pages or endpoints use `Astro.callAction()`, while client-side components can call actions directly.

In Astro 7, calling an action from a server context (like a `.astro` page component) requires using `Astro.callAction()` to ensure proper handling. Direct calls like `actions.logout()` are allowed in client code but not in server-rendered pages without this wrapper.

Both styles return the same result shape: `{ data, error }`.

Example of server usage:
```ts
const { data, error } = await Astro.callAction(actions.findProduct, { query: 'laptop' });
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/

From a **server endpoint**, use `Astro.callAction()` to invoke the action, returning `{ data, error }` objects.

From an **Astro page script during SSR**, also use `Astro.callAction()`, which returns the same `{ data, error }`.

From a **browser component**, call the action directly using `actions.myAction()` (imported from `'astro:actions'`) and handle the result via the client-side API.

All three locations require `Astro.callAction()` when invoked from server-rendered contexts to avoid `ActionCalledFromServerError`.

The action is being called correctly and returning a result, but the UI isn't rendering because the page likely prerendered without the action result data.

In Astro 7, when using `Astro.getActionResult()` with form actions, if the page was prerendered (which happens by default for static sites), the action result won't be available until after the page is hydrated on the client side. The middleware approach described in the docs ensures that results persist across redirects and are accessible post-render.

To fix this, ensure your page uses `client:only` or similar hydration strategies to re-run logic after initial render, or implement session-based persistence as shown in the advanced example from the documentation.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/

Your form is missing `enctype="multipart/form-data"`, which is required for file uploads to be properly parsed and validated by Astro actions.

When a form contains `<input type="file">`, it must use `enctype="multipart/form-data"` to ensure that the browser sends the file data in a format that can be correctly interpreted by the action handler. Without this, the file input will not be included in the submitted FormData, causing validation to fail even if a file was selected.

Update your form like so:
```astro
<form enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <input type="file" name="file" />
  <button>Upload</button>
</form>
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/

You should use a plain `<form method="POST" action={actions.newsletter}>` on an on-demand page when you want to submit data without JavaScript, as a fallback, or for server-only handling. This approach requires no client-side script and relies entirely on the browser’s form submission mechanism.

In contrast, invoking actions from component scripts (e.g., using `await actions.newsletter()`) allows for richer interactivity but requires JavaScript and is not suitable for pages that are prerendered or require zero-JS behavior.

Both approaches work with `Astro.getActionResult()` to retrieve results on the server. However, form submissions via `<form action={...}>` must be on-demand rendered (not prerendered), while script-based actions can run in any rendering mode.

Example of a form submission:
```astro
<form method="POST" action={actions.newsletter}>
  <input type="email" name="email" />
  <button>Sign up</button>
</form>
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/

For actions with `accept: 'form'`, using plain `z.string()` is insufficient for certain HTML input types that require specific Zod validators to correctly parse and validate their values.

- **`type="number"`**: Should use `z.number()` to properly validate numeric input.
- **`type="checkbox"`**: Should use `z.coerce.boolean()` because its value is submitted as a string (`"on"` or `""`) and needs coercion to boolean.
- **`type="file"`**: Should use `z.instanceof(File)` to validate file inputs.
- **Multiple inputs with the same `name` attribute**: Should use `z.array(/* validator */)` to collect and validate multiple values.

Using `z.string()` for these types will not correctly parse or validate their data, potentially leading to runtime errors or incorrect validation behavior. Astro provides special handling for these cases under the hood when using form actions, but explicit validators must be used in your schema definition.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/

The `action` attribute on a form with `method="POST"` causes the browser to submit the form data to the server at the URL specified by `action={actions.logout}`. In Astro, this resolves to a special query string-based endpoint that routes the request to your defined action handler.

When you write `<form method="POST" action={actions.logout}>`, the browser sends a POST request to an internal Astro route that corresponds to your logout action. This route is automatically generated by Astro's actions system and handles form submissions without requiring JavaScript on the client-side.

The actual execution of your `logout` handler happens server-side when the request reaches this endpoint, where Astro processes it through its action pipeline using `Astro.getActionResult()` to retrieve the result for any necessary redirects or error handling. The form submission is handled entirely by Astro's internal routing and action processing system.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/

The `app.use('/dashboard', requireAuth)` middleware applies to the exact path `/dashboard` (e.g., `https://example.com/dashboard`) but not to its subpaths like `/dashboard/page`. The `app.use('/dashboard/*', requireAuth)` covers all requests under the `/dashboard` prefix, including nested paths such as `/dashboard/page`, `/dashboard/api/users`.

If you delete one of these lines:
- Removing `app.use('/dashboard', requireAuth)` would allow direct access to `/dashboard` without authentication.
- Removing `app.use('/dashboard/*', requireAuth)` would permit access to all subpaths under `/dashboard` (e.g., `/dashboard/page`, `/dashboard/api/users`) without requiring a valid session.

Both are necessary for comprehensive protection of the entire `/dashboard` route hierarchy. Deleting either could expose routes that should be protected, allowing unauthorized users to bypass authentication checks on specific paths.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/authentication/

When a visitor who isn't signed in accesses a route, `Astro.session` is `undefined`, so accessing `session.user?.name` returns `undefined` without error. This behavior occurs because sessions are only created for authenticated users or when explicitly used in on-demand rendered routes.

If the session is disabled or no session storage is configured, `Astro.session` will also be `undefined`. In such cases, attempting to access session data results in a runtime error unless defensive coding practices like optional chaining (`?.`) are used. The absence of an error indicates that sessions are properly enabled and initialized but simply contain no data for the unauthenticated visitor.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/api-reference/#session

Astro requires server endpoints to be in `src/pages/api/` for automatic mounting. Your Firebase authentication endpoints should reside at:

The Scalekit integration requires `output: 'server'` in `astro.config.mjs` because it uses server-side API routes (`src/pages/api/`) to handle sensitive operations like exchanging an authorization code for tokens. When `ASTRO_DEV_BACKGROUND=0` is set and `astro dev` is run on macOS with an AI coding agent detected, the existing background server continues running in the background. The new command does not stop or modify the existing server.

The lock file at `.astro/dev.json` remains unchanged and retains the original server’s URL, port, and PID. Running `astro dev` again with `ASTRO_DEV_BACKGROUND=0` will not affect the already-running background process or its lock file.

If you want to stop the background server, manually kill it using its PID from the lock file or use `astro dev --force` to terminate it before starting a new one in the foreground. The lock file is only updated when a new server starts and writes its own information.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/cli-reference/

This endpoint serves AI coding agents by providing a simple way to programmatically check whether the dev server is ready to accept requests, ensuring that the agent can safely interact with the server once it's fully initialized.

This is preferred because `astro add` handles installation, configuration, and dependency management in one step, ensuring compatibility and proper setup. It also verifies that the integration aligns with current Astro best practices and framework requirements, reducing the risk of misconfigurations or outdated patterns.

Astro starts a new server when `astro dev` is run with an AI agent detected on Linux, even if the `.astro/dev.json` lock file exists but references a non-running process. The mechanism that determines this behavior is the automatic background mode feature introduced in Astro 7.0.0, which detects AI agents and runs the dev server as a detached background process.

When `astro dev` starts with the `--background` flag (automatically applied when an AI agent is detected), it checks for existing servers by reading the lock file (`dev.json`) but does not block or report conflicts if the recorded PID no longer corresponds to a running process. Instead, it proceeds to start a new server instance and updates the lock file with the new PID.

This behavior avoids launching multiple instances of the dev server for the same project while ensuring that AI agents can operate without being blocked by foreground processes.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/cli-reference/#--background

When a route rule sets `tags: ['products']` and the route handler calls `Astro.cache.set({ tags: ['featured'] })`, the response gets **both tags**. Route-level cache settings merge with per-route calls to `cache.set()`. The final cache tags are the union of both sources.

Example:

```astro
---// Config sets tags: ['products']
// Handler adds tags: ['featured']
Astro.cache.set({ tags: ['featured'] });
---
```

Resulting tags: `['products', 'featured']`

The error occurs because the configured cache provider's `invalidate()` method does not support path-based invalidation. The `InvalidateOptions.path` property is only supported when the provider implements logic to handle exact-path purges, which many custom providers — especially CDN-style ones — don't implement.

To fix this, ensure your custom provider’s `invalidate()` function handles the `path` option by implementing logic that removes cached entries matching that path. Alternatively, use tag-based invalidation instead:

```ts
cache.invalidate({ tags: ['api-users'] });
```

To preserve the cache across deployments when using the Cloudflare adapter’s `cacheCloudflare()` provider, you would configure the [Cache TTL](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/cache/configuration/#cache-ttl) or use [Cache Tags](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/cache/configuration/#cache-tags) in your Worker script settings.

Example of setting TTL in your `wrangler.toml`:
```toml
[env.production]
name = "my-worker"
compatibility_date = "2023-10-01"

[[kv_namespaces]]
binding = "CACHE_NAMESPACE"
id = "your-kv-id"

# Configure cache behavior via Worker script or Wrangler settings
```

The `export const prerender = false;` declaration prevents the page from being statically generated at build time, ensuring it's rendered dynamically on each request when using server-side rendering (SSR) or API routes. In 'server' mode, this export is unnecessary because Astro automatically disables prerendering for pages that use `Astro.cache.set()`.

In 'server' mode, the page runs on the server and uses caching via the adapter's CDN provider (`cacheNetlify`, `cacheVercel`, etc.), which handles cache directives at the edge. The `prerender = false` export is redundant because Astro automatically disables prerendering for such pages in SSR mode.

Example:
```astro
---
export const prerender = false;
Astro.cache.set({
  maxAge: 120,
  swr: 60,
  tags: ['home'],
});
---
<html><body>Cached page</body></html>
```

When a CMS content update occurs, you should invalidate the cached entries using `cache.invalidate()` rather than changing the options passed to `cache.set()`.

Invalidating cache entries removes stale data from the cache so that fresh content is served on the next request. This ensures users see updated content immediately after a CMS change.

Changing options in `cache.set()` only affects future requests, not already cached responses. If you modify caching behavior without invalidating existing entries, outdated content may still be returned until the cache expires naturally or is manually cleared.

Use `cache.invalidate({ tags: ['content-tag'] })` to remove all cached pages associated with that tag (e.g., a specific blog post or product). Alternatively, use `cache.invalidate({ path: '/updated-page' })` for exact-path invalidation.

Example:
```ts
// Invalidate by tag after CMS update
await context.cache.invalidate({ tags: ['blog-post-123'] });
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/api-reference/#cacheinvalidate

Yes, you can pass multiple tags to `cache.invalidate({ tags: ['data', 'api'] })` at once. It invalidates all cached entries that have **any** of the provided tags, not just entries with all of them.

This behavior is consistent across Astro’s cache providers and matches the semantics described in the [Cache Provider API reference](https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/cache-provider-reference/#invalidateoptions).

Example:
```ts
await context.cache.invalidate({ tags: ['data', 'api'] });
```
This purges all cached entries tagged with either `'data'` or `'api'`.

However, Vercel’s ISR mechanism uses its own internal caching layer that operates independently of Astro’s cache provider.

Vercel caches pages based on the deployment lifecycle and ISR configuration (`expiration`, `exclude`, etc.), not just tags from Astro’s invalidation logic. Even if you invalidate a tag in Astro, Vercel may still serve cached content unless it's revalidated by an on-demand request or expiration time elapses.

To ensure immediate updates with ISR, use [on-demand invalidation](https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/vercel/#on-demand-invalidation) via the `x-prerender-revalidate` header and bypass token.

In Astro, a bare `<script>` tag without attributes is rendered directly as declared in the `.astro` file, matching the new default behavior starting in Astro v5.

Before Astro v5, script tags were hoisted to the `<head>` and bundled together. In Astro 5+, scripts are no longer hoisted or bundled; they're rendered exactly where you write them in the component, which can affect CSS styling if not handled carefully.

If a script is conditionally rendered (e.g., inside an `{if}` block), it will be included only when that condition evaluates to true. If you need such scripts to behave like v4.x (implicitly inlined), use `is:inline` attribute on the `<script>` tag.

Example:
```astro
{showAlert && <script is:inline>alert("Important message")</script>}
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/upgrade-to/v5/

This is because Astro only processes scripts that have no attributes besides `src`. To restore script processing, remove the `defer` attribute and use `hoist` instead (Astro 7+). Alternatively, wrap your script in a `<script is:inline>` tag to skip processing intentionally.

Example:
```astro
<script hoist>
  import confetti from 'canvas-confetti';
</script>
```

2. **`public/legacy-widget.js`** - Use `is:inline` directive to skip processing:

Astro deduplicates scripts by including each unique script only once per page, even if it’s imported multiple times across different components. If `src/scripts/track.ts` is imported in multiple `<script>` tags, Astro will bundle and inline it once.

Side effects from the module (like global variable assignments or console logs) are executed only once when the script is first loaded, not on each import. This behavior ensures that scripts with side effects run exactly once per page load, regardless of how many times they’re imported.

Example:
```astro
<!-- In component A -->
<script>
  import '../scripts/track.ts';
</script>

<!-- In component B -->
<script>
  import '../scripts/track.ts';
</script>
```

Both imports result in a single execution of `track.ts`'s side effects.

The global event listener will be registered only once, because Astro processes and deduplicates scripts across all instances of the same component on a page.

When you use `window.addEventListener('resize', handler)` inside a processed `<script>` tag within a component that is rendered multiple times (e.g., three times), Astro bundles and executes the script only once per page. This means the event listener is added just once, even though the component appears three times in the DOM.

This behavior ensures efficient resource usage by avoiding duplicate event listeners from being attached to the same global object (`window`) across multiple component instances. If you need a listener per instance (e.g., for component-specific logic), use `this.addEventListener()` inside custom elements or manage listeners manually within each component's scope using `connectedCallback` and cleanup in `disconnectedCallback`.

Using an official Astro integration eliminates the need to manually fetch and transform content data in your components, as the integration handles this automatically during the build process.

The integration manages data fetching, processing, and hydration for you. It also ensures proper TypeScript support and optimizes how content is rendered within Astro’s static site generation or server-side rendering workflows.

In contrast, using a JavaScript SDK directly requires writing custom logic in your components to fetch and format content manually — this increases complexity and can lead to performance issues if not handled carefully.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/mdx/

The final HTML that visitors receive is rendered by Astro, not the CMS.

In a headless CMS setup, the CMS handles content creation and management but does not generate the presentation layer. Instead, Astro fetches the content data from the CMS via its API and uses that data to build and render the final HTML pages. This allows Astro's features like server-side rendering (SSR), static site generation (SSG), and client-side hydration to take effect.

For example, when using Statamic or WordPress as a headless CMS with Astro:
- You fetch content through their REST or GraphQL APIs.
- Astro processes this data during the build process or at runtime.
- The resulting HTML is served by your chosen deployment platform — not directly from the CMS itself.

This architecture gives you full control over how content appears and behaves on your site, leveraging Astro's performance optimizations while keeping content management separate.

Astro’s static generation model requires all data to be fetched at build time, so if a CMS API is unavailable during a production build, the build will fail. This contrasts with server-rendered frameworks like Next.js or Nuxt, which can fetch data at request time on the server, tolerating temporary outages.

In Astro, `getStaticPaths()` and data fetching in `.astro` files must succeed at build time. If your CMS integration fails during this phase, you’ll get an error like “Module is only available server-side” or a runtime failure if using SSR (though SSR isn’t the default for static sites). You can avoid such failures by pre-fetching content locally or mocking data in development.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/server-only-module/

During an Astro 7 static site build, if a headless CMS API returns a 500 error for a content request, the build will fail completely, not skip the page or retry automatically. The error will be logged in the terminal during the build process, and you’ll see it reported as part of the build failure.

Astro does not provide a mechanism to gracefully handle such errors during static builds — if an error occurs while fetching content for a page (e.g., from a CMS), the build stops immediately. If you have a custom `500.astro` page, it won't be used in this scenario because that page is only rendered on-demand for runtime errors.

To avoid such failures, ensure your CMS API is stable or implement pre-build checks to validate content availability before starting the Astro build process.

This approach allows you to retrieve content from any REST API at build time. For example: ```astro --- // src/pages/index.astro const res = await fetch('https://[YOUR-SITE]/api/posts'); const posts = await res.json(); ---

When Astro builds a static site that sources content from a headless CMS, the fetch happens **during `astro build`**, not at request time or during `astro dev`. This is the default behavior for prerendered pages. The fetched content is then embedded into the final HTML files generated by the build process.

In contrast, server-rendered frameworks typically fetch content **at request time** on the hosting platform — meaning each visitor’s request triggers a new fetch from the CMS. Astro's approach differs because it pre-fetches and embeds content at build time, resulting in faster initial page loads and reduced reliance on runtime infrastructure for content delivery.

The most likely explanation is that your Astro project is using a static site generation (SSG) build process and hasn't been rebuilt to fetch the latest content from your headless CMS.

In Astro, when you use a headless CMS like Drupal or Statamic, the content is fetched at build time. If you've added new content in your CMS but haven't triggered a rebuild of your Astro site, it will continue to serve the old static version that was generated during the last build.

To resolve this:

2. Ensure your deployment pipeline fetches fresh data from the CMS on each deploy (e.g., using Netlify's build hooks or GitHub Actions)
3. If you're using a CDN, clear its cache

Example: ```astro --- import { getLiveCollection } from 'astro:content'; const posts = await getLiveCollection('posts'); ---
    {posts.map(post =>
  • {post.data.title}
    • )}
``` This page must be rendered on demand and requires an adapter like `@astrojs/node` or `@astrojs/netlify`. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/on-demand-rendering/
